{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_sb7unZC6tWp7q5ugOQCt7Zg0\", \"content\": \"\\n[Paper Details]\\nIdentifier: 2309.17453\\nIdentifier Type: arxiv\\n\\n==============================\\n   1: \\n   2: 1 Introduction\\n   3: Large Language Models (LLMs)~\\\\cite{bib.bib41, bib.bib10, bib.bib61, bib.bib36, bib.bib51, bib.bib52} are becoming ubiquitous, powering many natural language processing applications such as dialog systems~\\\\cite{bib.bib45, bib.bib47, bib.bib13}, document summarization~\\\\cite{bib.bib24, bib.bib62}, code completion~\\\\cite{bib.bib11, bib.bib43} and question answering~\\\\cite{bib.bib29}.  To unleash the full potential of pretrained LLMs, they should be able to efficiently and accurately perform long sequence generation.  For example, an ideal ChatBot assistant can stably work over the content of recent day-long conversations.  However, it is very challenging for LLM to generalize to longer sequence lengths than they have been pretrained on, e. g. , 4K for Llama-2~\\\\cite{bib.bib52}. \\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: The reason is that LLMs are constrained by the attention window during pre-training.  Despite substantial efforts to expand this window size~\\\\cite{bib.bib12, bib.bib28, bib.bib38} and improve training~\\\\cite{bib.bib17, bib.bib16} and inference~\\\\cite{bib.bib39, bib.bib56, bib.bib3, bib.bib53, bib.bib63} efficiency for lengthy inputs, the acceptable sequence length remains intrinsically finite, which doesn\u2019t allow persistent deployments. \\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: In this paper, we first introduce the concept of LLM streaming applications and ask the question:\\n  10: Can we deploy an LLM for infinite-length inputs without sacrificing efficiency and performance?\\n  11: When applying LLMs for infinite input streams, two primary challenges arise:\\n  12: \\n  13: 1. \\n  14: \\n  15: During the decoding stage, Transformer-based LLMs cache the Key and Value states (KV) of all previous tokens, as illustrated in Figure (a), which can lead to excessive memory usage and increasing decoding latency~\\\\cite{bib.bib39}. \\n  16: \\n  17: 2. \\n  18: \\n  19: Existing models have limited length extrapolation abilities, i. e. , their performance degrades~\\\\cite{bib.bib40, bib.bib12} when the sequence length goes beyond the attention window size set during pre-training. \\n  20: \\n  21: \\n  22: An intuitive approach, known as window attention~\\\\cite{bib.bib5} (Figure b), maintains only a fixed-size sliding window on the KV states of most recent tokens.  Although it ensures constant memory usage and decoding speed after the cache is initially filled, the model collapses once the sequence length exceeds the cache size, i. e. , even just evicting the KV of the first token, as illustrated in Figure. \\n  23: Another strategy is the sliding window with re-computation (shown in Figure c), which rebuilds the KV states of recent tokens for each generated token.  While it offers strong performance, this approach is significantly slower due to the computation of quadratic attention within its window, making this method impractical for real-world streaming applications. \\n  24: \\n  25: \\n  26: \\n  27: To understand the failure of window attention, we find an interesting phenomenon of autoregressive LLMs: a surprisingly large amount of attention score is allocated to the initial tokens, irrespective of their relevance to the language modeling task, as visualized in Figure.  We term these tokens \u201cattention sinks\\\". \\n  28: Despite their lack of semantic significance, they collect significant attention scores.  We attribute the reason to the Softmax operation, which requires attention scores to sum up to one for all contextual tokens.  Thus, even when the current query does not have a strong match in many previous tokens, the model still needs to allocate these unneeded attention values somewhere so it sums up to one.  The reason behind initial tokens as sink tokens is intuitive: initial tokens are visible to almost all subsequent tokens because of the autoregressive language modeling nature, making them more readily trained to serve as attention sinks. \\n  29: \\n  30: \\n  31: Based on the above insights, we propose StreamingLLM, a simple and efficient framework that enables LLMs trained with a finite attention window to work on text of infinite length without fine-tuning.  StreamingLLM exploits the fact that attention sinks have high attention values, and preserving them can maintain the attention score distribution close to normal.  Therefore, StreamingLLM simply keeps the attention sink tokens\u2019 KV (with just 4 initial tokens sufficing) together with the sliding window\u2019s KV to anchor the attention computation and stabilize the model\u2019s performance.  With StreamingLLM, models including Llama-2-[7, 13, 70]B, MPT-[7, 30]B, Falcon-[7, 40]B, and Pythia-[2.9,6.9,12]B can reliably model 4 million tokens, and potentially even more.  Compared with the only viable baseline, sliding window with recomputation, StreamingLLM achieves up to 22.2\u00d7\\\\times speedup, realizing the streaming use of LLMs. \\n  32: \\n  33: \\n  34: Furthermore, we confirm our attention sink hypothesis and demonstrate that language models can be pre-trained to require only a single attention sink token for streaming deployment. \\n  35: Specifically, we suggest that an extra learnable token at the beginning of all training samples can serve as a designated attention sink. \\n  36: By pre-training 160-million parameter language models from scratch, we demonstrate that adding this single sink token preserves the model\u2019s performance in streaming cases.  This stands in contrast to vanilla models, which necessitate the reintroduction of multiple initial tokens as attention sinks to achieve the same performance level. \\n  37: \\n  38: \\n  39: \\n  40: Finally, we emphasize that StreamingLLM efficiently generates coherent text from tokens within the KV cache without extending the LLMs\u2019 context length.  It suits continuous operation needs with minimal memory use and past data reliance.  Additionally, StreamingLLM can complement context extension methods to increase the attendable recent context.\\n  41: \\n  42: \\n  43: 2 Related Work\\n  44: Extensive research has been done on applying LLMs to lengthy texts, with three main areas of focus: Length Extrapolation, Context Window Extension, and Improving LLMs\u2019 Utilization of Long Text.  While seemingly related, it\u2019s worth noting that progress in one direction doesn\u2019t necessarily lead to progress in the other.  For example, extending the context size of LLMs doesn\u2019t improve the model\u2019s performance beyond the context size, and neither approach ensures effective use of the long context.  Our StreamingLLM framework primarily lies in the first category, where LLMs are applied to text significantly exceeding the pre-training window size, potentially even of infinite length.  We do not expand the attention window size of LLMs or enhance the model\u2019s memory and usage on long texts.  The last two categories are orthogonal to our focus and could be integrated with our techniques. \\n  45: \\n  46: \\n  47: Length extrapolation aims to enable language models trained on shorter texts to handle longer ones during testing.  A predominant avenue of research targets the development of relative position encoding methods for Transformer models, enabling them to function beyond their training window.  One such initiative is Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE)~\\\\cite{bib.bib46}, which transforms the queries and keys in every attention layer for relative position integration.  Despite its promise, subsequent research~\\\\cite{bib.bib40, bib.bib12} indicated its underperformance on text that exceeds the training window.  Another approach, ALiBi~\\\\cite{bib.bib40}, biases the query-key attention scores based on their distance, thereby introducing relative positional information.  While this exhibited improved extrapolation, our tests on MPT models highlighted a breakdown when the text length was vastly greater than the training length.  Current methodologies, however, have yet to achieve infinite length extrapolation, causing no existing LLMs to fit for streaming applications. \\n  48: \\n  49: \\n  50: Context Window Extension centers on expanding the LLMs\u2019 context window, enabling the processing of more tokens in one forward pass.  A primary line of work addresses the training efficiency problem.  Given the attention to computation\u2019s quadratic complexity during training, developing a long-context LLM is both a computational and memory challenge.  Solutions have ranged from system-focused optimizations like FlashAttention~\\\\cite{bib.bib17, bib.bib16}, which accelerates attention computation and reduces memory footprint, to approximate attention methods~\\\\cite{bib.bib59, bib.bib5, bib.bib54, bib.bib30} that trade model quality for efficiency.  Recently, there has been a surge of work on extending pre-trained LLMs with RoPE~\\\\cite{bib.bib12, bib.bib28, bib.bib8, bib.bib38}, involving position interpolation and fine-tuning.  However, all the aforementioned techniques only extend LLMs\u2019 context window to a limited extent, which falls short of our paper\u2019s primary concern of handling limitless inputs. \\n  51: \\n  52: \\n  53: Improving LLMs\u2019 Utilization of Long Text optimizes LLMs to better capture and employ the content within the context rather than merely taking them as inputs.  As highlighted by ~\\\\cite{bib.bib33} and ~\\\\cite{bib.bib32}, success in the previously mentioned two directions does not necessarily translate to competent utilization of lengthy contexts.  Addressing this effective usage of prolonged contexts within LLMs is still a challenge.  Our work concentrates on stably harnessing the most recent tokens, enabling the seamless streaming application of LLMs.\\n  54: \\n  55: \\n  56: 3 StreamingLLM 3.1 The Failure of Window Attention and Attention Sinks\\n  57: While the window attention technique offers efficiency during inference, it results in an exceedingly high language modeling perplexity.  Consequently, the model\u2019s performance is unsuitable for deployment in streaming applications.  In this section, we use the concept of attention sink to explain the failure of window attention, serving as the inspiration behind StreamingLLM.Figure shows the perplexity of language modeling on a 20K token text.  It is evident that perplexity spikes when the text length surpasses the cache size, led by the exclusion of initial tokens.  This suggests that the initial tokens, regardless of their distance from the predicted tokens, are crucial for maintaining the stability of LLMs.We visualize attention maps from all layers and heads of the Llama-2-7B and models in Figure.  We find that, beyond the bottom two layers, the model consistently focuses on the initial tokens across all layers and heads.  The implication is clear: removing these initial tokens\u2019 KV will remove a considerable portion of the denominator in the SoftMax function (Equation) in attention computation.  This alteration leads to a significant shift in the distribution of attention scores away from what would be expected in normal inference settings. \\n  58: \\n  59: \\n  60: \\n  61: SoftMax(x)i=exiex1+\u2211j=2Nexj,x1\u226bxj,j\u22082,\u2026,N\\\\text{SoftMax}(x)_{i}=\\\\frac{e^{x_{i}}}{e^{x_{1}}+\\\\sum_{j=2}^{N}e^{x_{j}}},\\\\quad x_{1}\\\\gg x_{j},j\\\\in 2,\\\\dots,N\\n  62: \\n  63: (1)\\n  64: \\n  65: \\n  66: \\n  67: There are two possible explanations for the importance of the initial tokens in language modeling: (1) Either their semantics are crucial, or\\n  68: (2) the model learns a bias towards their absolute position.  To distinguish between these possibilities, we conduct experiments (Table), wherein the first four tokens are substituted with the linebreak token \u201c\\\\n\\\".  The observations indicate that the model still significantly emphasizes these initial linebreak tokens.  Furthermore, reintroducing them restores the language modeling perplexity to levels comparable to having the original initial tokens.  This suggests that the absolute position of the starting tokens, rather than their semantic value, holds greater significance.To explain why the model disproportionately focuses on initial tokens\u2014regardless of their semantic relevance to language modeling, we introduce the concept of \u201cattention sink\\\".  The nature of the SoftMax function (Equation) prevents all attended tokens from having zero values.  This requires aggregating some information from other tokens across all heads in all layers, even if the current embedding has sufficient self-contained information for its prediction.  Consequently, the model tends to dump unnecessary attention values to specific tokens.  A similar observation has been made in the realm of quantization outliers~\\\\cite{bib.bib56, bib.bib9}, leading to the proposal of SoftMax-Off-by-One~\\\\cite{bib.bib35} as a potential remedy. \\n  69: \\n  70: \\n  71: \\n  72: \\n  73: \\n  74: \\n  75: \\n  76: \\n  77: \\n  78: \\n  79: \\n  80: \\n  81: \\n  82: \\n  83: \\n  84: \\n  85: \\n  86: \\n  87: \\n  88: \\n  89: \\n  90: \\n  91: \\n  92: \\n  93: \\n  94: \\n  95: \\n  96: \\n  97: \\n  98: \\n  99: \\n 100: \\n 101: \\n 102: \\n 103: \\n 104: \\n 105: \\n 106: \\n 107: \\n 108: \\n 109: \\n 110: \\n 111: \\n 112: \\n 113: \\n 114: \\n 115: \\n 116: \\n 117: \\n 118: \\n 119: \\n 120: \\n 121: \\n 122: \\n 123: \\n 124: \\n 125: \\n 126: \\n 127: \\n 128: \\n 129: \\n 130: \\n 131: \\n 132: \\n 133: \\n 134: \\n 135: \\n 136: \\n 137: \\n 138: \\n 139: \\n 140: \\n 141: Why do various autoregressive LLMs, such as Llama-2, MPT, Falcon, and Pythia, consistently focus on initial tokens as their attention sinks, rather than other tokens? Our explanation is straightforward: Due to the sequential nature of autoregressive language modeling, initial tokens are visible to all subsequent tokens, while later tokens are only visible to a limited set of subsequent tokens.  As a result, initial tokens are more easily trained to serve as attention sinks, capturing unnecessary attention. \\n 142: \\n 143: \\n 144: We\u2019ve noted that LLMs are typically trained to utilize multiple initial tokens as attention sinks rather than just one.  As illustrated in Figure, the introduction of four initial tokens, as attention sinks, suffices to restore the LLM\u2019s performance.  In contrast, adding just one or two doesn\u2019t achieve full recovery.  We believe this pattern emerges because these models didn\u2019t include a consistent starting token across all input samples during pre-training.  Although Llama-2 does prefix each paragraph with a \u201c<s>\\\" token, it\u2019s applied before text chunking, resulting in a mostly random token occupying the zeroth position.  This lack of a uniform starting token leads the model to use several initial tokens as attention sinks.  We hypothesize that by incorporating a stable learnable token at the start of all training samples, it could singularly act as a committed attention sink, eliminating the need for multiple initial tokens to ensure consistent streaming.  We will validate this hypothesis in Section.\\n 145: \\n 146: \\n 147: 3 StreamingLLM 3.2 Rolling KV Cache with Attention Sinks\\n 148: To enable LLM streaming in already trained LLMs, we propose a straightforward method that can recover window attention\u2019s perplexity without any model finetuning.  Alongside the current sliding window tokens, we reintroduce a few starting tokens\u2019 KV in the attention computation.  The KV cache in StreamingLLM can be conceptually divided into two parts, as illustrated in Figure: (1) Attention sinks (four initial tokens) stabilize the attention computation; 2) Rolling KV Cache retains the most recent tokens, crucial for language modeling.  StreamingLLM\u2019 design is versatile and can be seamlessly incorporated into any autoregressive language model that employs relative positional encoding, such as RoPE~\\\\cite{bib.bib46} and ALiBi~\\\\cite{bib.bib40}. \\n 149: \\n 150: \\n 151: When determining the relative distance and adding positional information to tokens, StreamingLLM focuses on positions within the cache rather than those in the original text.  This distinction is crucial for StreamingLLM\u2019s performance.  For instance, if the current cache (Figure) has tokens [0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8] and is in the process of decoding the 9th token, the positions assigned are [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], rather than the positions in the original text, which would be [0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9]. \\n 152: \\n 153: \\n 154: For encoding like RoPE, we cache the Keys of tokens prior to introducing the rotary transformation.  Then, we apply position transformation to the keys in the rolling cache at each decoding phase.  On the other hand, integrating with ALiBi is more direct.  Here, the contiguous linear bias is applied instead of a \u2019jumping\u2019 bias to the attention scores.  This method of assigning positional embedding within the cache is crucial to StreamingLLM\u2019s functionality, ensuring that the model operates efficiently even beyond its pre-training attention window size.\\n 155: \\n 156: \\n 157: 3 StreamingLLM 3.3 Pre-Training LLMs with Attention Sinks\\n 158: As elaborated in Section, a significant reason for the model\u2019s excessive attention to multiple initial tokens is the absence of a designated sink token to offload excessive attention scores.  Due to this, the model inadvertently uses globally visible tokens, primarily the initial ones, as attention sinks.  A potential remedy can be the intentional inclusion of a global trainable attention sink token, denoted as a \u201cSink Token\u201d, which would serve as a repository for unnecessary attention scores.  Alternatively, replacing the conventional SoftMax function with a variant like SoftMax-off-by-One~\\\\cite{bib.bib35},\\n 159: \\n 160: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__paper_search__get_paper_fulltext\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

The effect has been observed across training stages and hyperparameters ~\\\\cite{bib.bib2, bib.bib15}, across model families and datasets ~\\\\cite{bib.bib6}, and under diverse positional encodings\u2014including ALiBi ~\\\\cite{bib.bib5}, RoPE ~\\\\cite{bib.bib4}, and even no explicit positional encodings ~\\\\cite{bib.bib2}.  Similar sink-like patterns have also been reported in large multimodal models and vision transformers ~\\\\cite{bib.bib10, bib.bib14, bib.bib11}. \\n   4: 1\\n   5:  \\n   6:  \\n   7:  \\n   8:  \\n   9:  \\n  10:  \\n  11:  \\n  12:  However, some architectures have been reported to have little to no sink ~\\\\cite{bib.bib18, bib.bib13}. \\n  13: \\n  14: \\n  15: The practical stakes are significant. Understanding when sinks arise and how to control them is therefore directly relevant for model performance and interpretability. \\n  16: \\n  17: \\n  18: We study the sink mechanistically in GPT-2\u2013style Transformers with learned query biases and absolute positional embeddings ~\\\\cite{bib.bib16}.  Combining structural analysis with targeted causal interventions validated across natural-language, mathematical, and code inputs, we tie the first-token sink to three interacting components: learned query bias, first-layer MLP transformation of the positional encoding, and structure in the key projection. \\n  19: 2\\n  20:  \\n  21:  \\n  22:  \\n  23:  \\n  24:  \\n  25:  \\n  26:  \\n  27:  Our findings connect to and extend a body of work on the origins of attention sinks; see Appendix for a discussion. This implies that while attention sinks are robust as a phenomenon, they are not governed by a single universal mechanism. \\n  31: Consequently, many post-training mitigations may need to be architecture-specific, and many pre-training architectural interventions may not generalize (see ). \\n  32: This highlights the need to understand why the sink emerges as a prerequisite for developing robust pre-training strategies.\\n  33: \\n  34: \\n  35: 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Attention mechanism\\n  36: We use DD for model dimension, HH for number of heads, DhD_{h} for per-head dimension, and LL for number of layers. We then provide empirical evidence through four analyses in , , and and confirm causality through targeted interventions in .\\n  67: \\n  68: \\n  69: 3 Methodology and Results 3.1 The Mechanism behind Attention Sinks\\n  70: Expanding the attention score si\u2192j,h(l)s_{i\\\\to j,h}^{(l)} (layer ll, head hh, source position ii, target position jj) from by substituting the expressions for qi,h(l)q_{i,h}^{(l)} and kj,h(l)k_{j,h}^{(l)} gives si\u2192j,h(l)=(xi(l)\u200bWq,h(l))\u200b(xj(l)\u200bWk,h(l))\u22a4+(xi(l)\u200bWq,h(l))\u200bbK,h(l)\u22a4+bQ,h(l)\u200b(xj(l)\u200bWk,h(l))\u22a4+bQ,h(l)\u200bbK,h(l)\u22a4s_{i\\\\to j,h}^{(l)}=\\\\bigl(x_{i}^{(l)}W_{q,h}^{(l)}\\\\bigr)\\\\bigl(x_{j}^{(l)}W_{k,h}^{(l)}\\\\bigr)^{\\\\top}+\\\\bigl(x_{i}^{(l)}W_{q,h}^{(l)}\\\\bigr)b_{K,h}^{(l)\\\\top}+b_{Q,h}^{(l)}\\\\bigl(x_{j}^{(l)}W_{k,h}^{(l)}\\\\bigr)^{\\\\top}+b_{Q,h}^{(l)}b_{K,h}^{(l)\\\\top}. \\n  71: The third term, \u0394j,h(l)\u225cbQ,h(l)\u200bWk,h(l)\u22a4\u200bxj(l)\u22a4\\\\Delta_{j,h}^{(l)}\\\\triangleq b_{Q,h}^{(l)}W_{k,h}^{(l)\\\\top}x_{j}^{(l)\\\\top}, is a token-specific, source-agnostic\\n  72: shift: it raises or lowers the score toward target position jj identically for every source position ii. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_xmCO685DaUU00D2umZTjUkUX\", \"content\": \"\\n[Paper Details]\\nIdentifier: 2606.08105\\nIdentifier Type: arxiv\\n\\n==============================\\n   1: \\n   2: 1 Introduction\\n   3: Attention sinks \u2013 tokens that attract disproportionate attention mass across many queries \u2013 are pervasive in softmax transformers~\\\\cite{bib.bib7}, especially vision transformers (ViTs)~\\\\cite{bib.bib5, bib.bib6, bib.bib9, bib.bib8} and large language models (LLMs)~\\\\cite{bib.bib34, bib.bib35, bib.bib36}.  Empirically, they appear as near-vertical \u201cstripes\u201d in attention maps~\\\\cite{bib.bib26, bib.bib18, bib.bib21, bib.bib28}, often at the [CLS] token or specific patch locations~\\\\cite{bib.bib4, bib.bib37, bib.bib44}.  Yet the same visual signature can reflect very different computations, raising a practical question: when we see a sink, what algorithm is the model executing, and what intervention should we apply?\\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: Related work has connected sink-like patterns to spectral concentration, rank collapse, anisotropy, massive activations, token-wise norm imbalance, and softmax saturation~\\\\cite{bib.bib40, bib.bib41, bib.bib21, bib.bib18, bib.bib28, bib.bib20, bib.bib38, bib.bib29, bib.bib39, bib.bib42}.  These effects can harm stability and representation quality~\\\\cite{bib.bib19}.  At the same time, sinks can be useful: in bidirectional attention, a token that aggregates and redistributes global information can act as a learned workspace~\\\\cite{bib.bib4}.  Thus, \u201cfixing\u201d sinks in ViTs without understanding their role risks either removing useful computation or missing the source of instability. \\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: The central challenge is that attention patterns alone are not mechanistic explanations~\\\\cite{bib.bib12, bib.bib11, bib.bib10}.  A softmax head must place probability mass somewhere, so concentrating on a sink can mean either that the sink is informative or that it is a safe destination when the head should do nothing~\\\\cite{bib.bib43}.  These cases can produce the same stripe: routing to a token with near-zero value norm implements an effective no-op (NOP) on the residual stream, while routing to a token with meaningful value broadcasts a shared component to many positions.  Interventions designed for one mechanism may therefore fail when the other is active. \\n  10: \\n  11: \\n  12: This perspective helps explain why the literature has not converged on a single mitigation.  Gating mechanisms~\\\\cite{bib.bib23} and register tokens~\\\\cite{bib.bib4} both reduce sink-like behavior, but differ fundamentally in design and, under our view, target different computations rather than one shared pathology.  What has been missing is a unified framing that separates these hypotheses, makes each identifiable in controlled settings, and yields diagnostics for determining which mechanism is operative in a given network, layer, or head.  We take this step by treating sinks as arising from two computationally distinct algorithms\u2014adaptive no-op (NOP) and broadcast\u2014and by proposing measurable signatures based on both attention structure and residual-stream statistics. \\n  13: \\n  14: \\n  15: Concretely, we develop a two-hypothesis view and connect each hypothesis to an intervention that targets it.  Under Adaptive NOP, sinks suppress residual updates, predicting near-zero sink value norms and spectral/activation signatures of hard gating.  Under Broadcast, sinks act as communication hubs, predicting non-negligible sink values, approximately low-rank attention outputs, and shared components across tokens.  We instantiate both mechanisms with minimal synthetic objectives, use them to develop diagnostics, and apply the resulting tools to pretrained ViTs, where we find that both mechanisms co-occur.  We further show that gated attention, which addresses NOP sinks, and register tokens, which support or regularize broadcast computation, provide complementary benefits. In that case, sinks serve an analogous role: a safe destination when there is nothing useful to compute. Proposed interventions like gating or registers work because they implicitly target one or the other, revealing a duality between method and assumed mechanism: gating implicitly assumes nop; registers implicitly assume broadcast. Each mechanism leaves distinct traces (nop sinks exhibit negligible value norms; broadcast sinks induce low-rank outputs) which we formalize on synthetic tasks and use to derive practical diagnostics. Combining gating with registers yields complementary gains in stability and performance. Attention Rows as Compositional Data\\n   Date: 2026-08-11\\n   Year: 2026\\n   ArXiv ID: 2608.14712v1\\n   Type: preprint\\n   Publication Status: preprint\\n   Repository: arXiv\\n   URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14712v1\\n   Abstract: Each row of a transformer's attention matrix is a probability distribution over tokens, and in trained models most of that probability lands on a single \\\\emph{sink} token, usually the first. Standard tools for comparing attention rows (cosine similarity, Jensen--Shannon divergence, Shannon entropy) therefore hinge on a choice papers rarely report: keep the sink, or drop it and renormalize. This choice can reverse conclusions. On ten pretrained models from five families, 17--47% of verdicts about which of two heads is more similar flip with the convention, and the most prominent structure in a standard BERT head-clustering pipeline is an artifact of it. The reason is that one-number summaries mix two questions: how much attention the sink takes, and how the rest is divided among the content tokens. Treating rows as compositional data separates them exactly: the Aitchison distance splits orthogonally into a sink term and a content term, entropy splits by an exact identity, and the content distance is characterized by invariances the transformer itself possesses. The separation matters in practice: most measured entropy collapse during training is the sink growing, not attention sharpening (30% of the drop at 70M parameters, 95% at 1B, 79% at 1.4B), and pruning heads with the wrong channel can inflate perplexity more than a hundredfold. We map where each convention is safe, test a frozen out-of-sample predictor (one confirmation, one abstention, one failure), and release code regenerating every number.\\n\\n2. \u3010ArXiv\u3011An Improved Attention for Visual Question Answering\\n   Date: 2021-06-07\\n   Year: 2021\\n   ArXiv ID: 2011.02164\\n   Type: preprint\\n   Publication Status: preprint\\n   Repository: arXiv\\n   URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.02164\\n   Abstract: We consider the problem of Visual Question Answering (VQA). Given an image and a free-form, open-ended, question, expressed in natural language, the goal of VQA system is to provide accurate answer to this question with respect to the image. The task is challenging because it requires simultaneous and intricate understanding of both visual and textual information. Attention, which captures intra- and inter-modal dependencies, has emerged as perhaps the most widely used mechanism for addressing these challenges. In this paper, we propose an improved attention-based architecture to solve VQA. We incorporate an Attention on Attention (AoA) module within encoder-decoder framework, which is able to determine the relation between attention results and queries. Attention module generates weighted average for each query. On the other hand, AoA module first generates an information vector and an attention gate using attention results and current context; and then adds another attention to generate final attended information by multiplying the two. We also propose multimodal fusion module to combine both visual and textual information. The goal of this fusion module is to dynamically decide how much information should be considered from each modality. Extensive experiments on VQA-v2 benchmark dataset show that our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance.\\n\\n3. \u3010ArXiv\u3011Self-Attention is All You Need\\n   Authors: [\\\"Stanford CS224N\\\",\\\"Default Project\\\",\\\"Joanne Zhou\\\",\\\"Brian Hill\\\",\\\"Vincent Li\\\"]\\n   Type: preprint\\n   Publication Status: preprint\\n   Repository: arXiv\\n   URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/\\n   Abstract: The internet contains the answer to most questions, the challenge mostly lies in finding it. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_pEJ8mKuUMut0L37aS6r2cpwJ\", \"content\": \"\\n[Paper Details]\\nIdentifier: 2608.14712\\nIdentifier Type: arxiv\\n\\n==============================\\n   1: \\n   2: 1 Introduction\\n   3: Softmax attention produces, for every query position, a probability distribution over keys, a point on the simplex.  This is precisely a composition in the sense of ~\\\\cite{bib.bib1}: a vector of positive parts carrying only relative information.  The interpretability and training-stability literatures routinely compare and summarize these rows.  ~\\\\cite{bib.bib10} cluster BERT heads by the JS divergence between attention rows; cosine similarity between attention maps is pervasive; ~\\\\cite{bib.bib14} track the Shannon entropy of attention rows to diagnose entropy collapse; head-role taxonomies and pruning scores ~\\\\cite{bib.bib13, bib.bib12, bib.bib21} summarize populations of attention rows with Euclidean averages.  These statistics are valid for their intended targets, but full-row comparisons need not preserve conclusions after a coordinate is removed and the row is renormalized, and Shannon entropy combines marginal sink mass with conditional content entropy.  Compositional data analysis (CoDA) identifies the properties at stake: perturbation invariance and subcompositional coherence ~\\\\cite{bib.bib1, bib.bib2, bib.bib3}. \\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: CoDA critiques of Euclidean statistics date back four decades.  What makes them consequential here is a second, recent empirical fact: attention mass concentrates overwhelmingly on a few sink coordinates, chiefly the first or \u27e8bos\u27e9\\\\\\\\{bos}\\\\ token ~\\\\cite{bib.bib16, bib.bib18, bib.bib19}.  In a typical Llama-3.1-405B prompt roughly 80%80\\\\% of the attention mass sits on the \u27e8bos\u27e9\\\\\\\\{bos}\\\\ token ~\\\\cite{bib.bib20}, and the fraction of sink heads grows with model scale ~\\\\cite{bib.bib19}.  A sink is exactly the kind of dominant shared part whose inclusion or exclusion CoDA warns changes Euclidean and divergence-based comparisons.  Whether an analysis keeps the sink column, or masks it and renormalizes, is today an undocumented analyst choice, and this choice can determine the answer: two heads that divide their non-sink attention identically can be scored as distant, and a head with the opposite content preference ranked their nearest neighbor, purely because all three share a large sink (Figure). \\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: Two estimands.  Full-row statistics answer questions about total allocation, sink included; sink-dropped statistics answer questions about allocation conditional on ignoring the sink. As their attention patterns are the only mechanism that allows for the mixing of information between tokens within a Transformer architecture, it is natural to study them to understand how information is being processed.  A peculiar and interesting phenomenon that has been spotted across frontier language models is that attention heads often exhibit \u2018attention sinks\u2019, where seemingly meaningless tokens \u2013 often the first one in the sequence \u2013 tend to capture most of the attention.  Attention sinks have been linked to a number of important topics such as quantisation ~\\\\cite{bib.bib18}, improved KV-caching ~\\\\cite{bib.bib12}, streaming attention ~\\\\cite{bib.bib30}, and even security vulnerabilities ~\\\\cite{bib.bib31}, making them an important artifact that is not yet well-understood in frontier LLMs. \\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: While many works have studied attention sinks in order to mitigate them, in this work we take a different angle and aim to understand why they are useful.  We do this for a simple reason: as sinks are widespread and appear as a byproduct of gradient descent rather than any explicit priors, they must provide an important mechanism for processing the context.  We are therefore interested in understanding and explaining when and why the attention sink mechanism is useful.  We tackle the issue from various angles: theoretically studying why such an effect is useful from a \u2018mixing\u2019 perspective, and performing measurements in both frontier LLMs and models we train from scratch to support our theory. \\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: We focus specifically on understanding why attention sinks occur mostly at the first position of the context.  In this position, there commonly lives a special token often denoted as \u27e8bos\u27e9\\\\\\\\text{bos}\\\\ (beginning of sequence).  We find, for example, that in a typical prompt in Llama 405B, almost 80%80\\\\% of the attention is concentrated on the \u27e8bos\u27e9\\\\\\\\text{bos}\\\\ token (see Section for details).  This type of attention allocation is in many ways \u2018wasted\u2019, and we find it intriguing to understand exactly why this type of learned behavior is useful. \\n  10: \\n  11: \\n  12: Our main contribution is showing that this type of pattern is a way for deep Transformers to avoid \u2018over-mixing\u2019, a phenomenon related to a number of theoretical and empirical works that study rank collapse ~\\\\cite{bib.bib10}, representational collapse ~\\\\cite{bib.bib2}, signal propagation ~\\\\cite{bib.bib20, bib.bib1}, and over-smoothing ~\\\\cite{bib.bib9}.  In particular, the depth and large context of modern LLMs seems to be sufficient to cause representational collapse, which can be slowed down by making certain heads inactive: a behaviour which attention sinks directly promote (see Figure ). {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_SYtykztmSOovsYngSHKjm8SH\", \"content\": \"Search sources: ArXiv, Google Scholar, Crossref (top 6 per source)\\nFound 14 papers (deduplicated and sorted by priority + time):\\n\\n1. \u3010ArXiv\u3011KVSink: Understanding and Enhancing the Preservation of Attention Sinks\\n  in KV Cache Quantization for LLMs\\n   Authors: Zunhai Su, Kehong Yuan\\n   Date: 2025-08-06\\n   Year: 2025\\n   ArXiv ID: 2508.04257v1\\n   Type: preprint\\n   Publication Status: preprint\\n   Repository: arXiv\\n   URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04257v1\\n   Abstract: Key-Value (KV) cache quantization has become a widely adopted optimization technique for efficient large language models (LLMs) inference by reducing KV cache memory usage and mitigating memory-bound constraints. Recent studies have emphasized the importance of preserving the original precision of KVs for the first few tokens to ensure the protection of attention sinks. While this approach has proven effective in mitigating performance degradation, its underlying principles remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, it fails to address the recent discovery that attention sinks can emerge beyond the initial token positions. In this work, we elucidate the underlying mechanisms of attention sinks during inference by examining their role in the cross-layer evolution of extreme activation outliers. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between attention sinks and KV cache quantization. Based on our enhanced understanding, we introduce \\\\textit{\\\\textbf{KVSink}}, a plug-and-play method that effectively predicts sink tokens with negligible overhead, enabling more thorough preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KVSink outperforms the existing Preserve-First-N (PFN) strategy, offering more effective preservation of attention sinks during KV cache quantization. Moreover, when applied to the well-established KVQuant method, KVSink further improves perplexity (PPL) and reduces reliance on 16-bit numerical outliers.\\n\\n2. \u3010ArXiv\u3011WeightedKV: Attention Scores Weighted Key-Value Cache Merging for Large\\n  Language Models\\n   Authors: Jian Yuan, Ziwei He, Haoli Bai, Jingwen Leng, Bo Jiang\\n   Date: 2025-03-03\\n   Year: 2025\\n   ArXiv ID: 2503.01330v1\\n   Type: preprint\\n   Publication Status: preprint\\n   Repository: arXiv\\n   URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01330v1\\n   Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) use key-value (KV) cache to reduce redundant computation in autoregressive generation. However, the KV cache size increases linearly during generation, leading to excessive memory usage, especially for long texts. Most KV cache compression methods evict the unimportant KV pairs to maintain a fixed cache size, which leads to the permanent loss of tokens during generation. (5 authors)\\n   Journal: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence\\n   Publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)\\n   Date: 2026-03-14\\n   Year: 2026\\n   DOI: 10.1609/aaai.v40i37.40422\\n   Citations: 1\\n   Volume: 40, Issue: 37, Pages: 31563-31572\\n   Type: journal-article\\n   ISSN: 2374-3468\\n   URL: https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v40i37.40422\\n   Abstract: <jats:p>The high memory demands of the Key-Value (KV) Cache during the inference of Large Language Models (LLMs) severely restrict their deployment in resource-constrained platforms. (7 authors)\\n   Journal: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME)\\n   Publisher: IEEE\\n   Date: 2025-06-30\\n   Year: 2025\\n   DOI: 10.1109/icme59968.2025.11209367\\n   Citations: 4\\n   Type: proceedings-article\\n   URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/icme59968.2025.11209367\\n\\n12. \u3010Crossref\u3011Key-Value Cache Quantization in Large Language Models: A Safety Benchmark\\n   Authors: Timothy Liu\\n   Journal: International Journal of Computer Science and Information Technology\\n   Publisher: Warwick Evans Publishing\\n   Date: 2024-10-10\\n   Year: 2024\\n   DOI: 10.62051/ijcsit.v4n2.16\\n   Volume: 4, Issue: 2, Pages: 107-113\\n   Type: journal-article\\n   ISSN: 3005-7140\\n   URL: https://doi.org/10.62051/ijcsit.v4n2.16\\n   Abstract: <jats:p>The misuse of large language models (LLMs) is an ongoing concern with the expansion of general public access to LLMs. One reason for expanded access is the development of key-value (KV) cache quantization, a technique that significantly reduces both the large computing resource requirements and memory bottlenecks that are characteristic of LLMs. As more developers and vendors begin to prioritize efficiency in LLM training, protective measures against the misuse of language models become more of an afterthought. To address the expected increase of LLM misuse accompanying KV cache quantization, this paper covers a proof-of-concept benchmark to evaluate the proficiency of LLMs in response safety when tested against a sample of unsafe questions consisting of 13 different question categories. Response safety is a model\u2019s ability to both clearly deny providing a response to a given question and avoid providing any additional information that attempts to provide an accurate answer. By testing the sample against the Meta Llama-2-7B pretrained chat model, we determine response safety fine-tuning considerations that address performance bias among the 13 question categories. We hope this study brings attention to not only the sacrifices of accuracy but also response safety of KV cache quantization in large language models. (Code and data are available at https://github.com/TimochiL/llm_benchmark.) Disclaimer: This paper contains examples of harmful language. Reader discretion is recommended.</jats:p>\\n\\n13. \u3010Crossref\u3011Dependable Operation of Large Language Models against Soft Memory Errors: The Quantized Key-Value (KV) Cache Scenario\\n   Authors: Zhen Gao, Jie Deng, Pedro Reviriego et al. (5 authors)\\n   Publisher: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)\\n   DOI: 10.36227/techrxiv.177219978.81733697/v1\\n   Type: posted-content\\n   URL: https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177219978.81733697/v1\\n   Abstract: <jats:p>The Transformer architecture has caused the widespread development of large language models (LLMs) for improving performance in a wide range of natural language processing tasks. One of the fundamental innovations of Transformers is the new mechanism referred to as Attention. Attention can capture complex relations among words in a text, but it requires significant computation; to address this issue, most LLMs implement a cache that stores the Keys and Values (known as KV cache) to avoid re-computation. This cache can be of significant size, sometimes even larger than for the LLM parameters and thus, it is critical for dependable operation, such as for example in the presence of soft memory errors. The impact of soft errors on the memory for KV cache has not been studied, so this paper considers errors on 8-bit and 4-bit quantized KV caches of a widely used LLM, LLaMA3 3B; an evaluation is pursued by fault injection, and the following valuable conclusions are drawn: 1) the Key cache is more robust to errors than the Value cache; 2) the two most significant bits (MSBs) are critical for the dependable operation of the KV cache; 3) errors increasing the amplitude of the values cause a larger performance loss. Based on these findings, we propose a selective protection scheme for the two MSBs; the proposed protection scheme for the KV cache is then integrated with those for embeddings and weights, to show that all the three memory components can be simultaneously protected.</jats:p>\\n\\n14. \u3010Crossref\u3011Breaking the Memory Wall: A Survey of Key-Value (KV) Cache Compression for Efficient Large Language Model (LLM) Inference&nbsp;\\n   Authors: Manpreet Singh, Yash Jajoo, Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu\\n   Publisher: Elsevier BV\\n   DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.7273098\\n   Type: posted-content\\n   URL: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7273098\\n   Abstract: <jats:p>The deployment of large language models (LLMs) at long context lengths is increasingly limited by memory rather than compute. During autoregressive decoding, the key-value (KV) cache stores the key and value activations of processed tokens, grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, and must often be streamed for each generated token. In long-context and high-throughput settings, this makes decoding memory-bandwidthbound and exposes the memory wall. This survey gives a unified, hardware-aware treatment of techniques that mitigate this bottleneck. We formalise it through the roofline model and a VRAM-footprint analysis separating compute-bound prefill from memorybound decoding, then organise the literature into four complementary layers: algorithmic compression (quantization, eviction and sparsification, and token, low-rank, or learned merging); architectural redesign (multi-query and grouped-query attention, low-rank latent attention, and recurrent or hybrid state-space models); system-level management (paged memory, prefix sharing, cross-request transport, and tiered offloading); and hardware acceleration (decoding kernels, fusion, and processing-in-memory). For each we give the governing mechanism, achievable memory reduction, and accuracy-latency trade-offs. Distinct from prior surveys, we (a) unify the four layers under a co-design and Pareto-frontier framework, (b) consolidate the evidence on multi-tenant KV cache security and side-channel leakage, and (c) analyse cache degradation in long-horizon agentic loops. To make this gap actionable, we propose Matched-Budget Evaluation (MBE), a lightweight reporting protocol and accompanying pilot harness for describing KV-cache results at fixed memory budgets. We present MBE as a standardization proposal, not a fully validated benchmark. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_wRcYXcl1bknyULaJLAIiP8LO\", \"content\": \"\\n[Paper Details]\\nIdentifier: 2502.15075\\nIdentifier Type: arxiv\\n\\n==============================\\n   1: \\n   2: 1 Introduction\\n   3: LLMs have introduced significant advancements to the capabilities of NLP via their ability to express and capture intricate ideas ~\\\\cite{bib.bib1, bib.bib2}, and a key reason for these advancements is model scaling.  GPT has seen a tremendous increase across its four versions: GPT-1 at 117M ~\\\\cite{bib.bib3}, GPT-2 at 1.5B ~\\\\cite{bib.bib4}, GPT-3 at 175B ~\\\\cite{bib.bib5}, and GPT-4 at 1.8T parameters ~\\\\cite{bib.bib6}.  In the open-source space, Llama has grown to 2T ~\\\\cite{bib.bib7}, Mistral Large is now 123B ~\\\\cite{bib.bib8}, and DeepSeek V3 is at 671B ~\\\\cite{bib.bib9}. \\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: However, with this growth in model size comes a prohibitive memory bottleneck in the KV cache ~\\\\cite{bib.bib10}.  An increase in parameter count requires an increase in context-window length to accommodate chain-of-thought reasoning, which in turn expands the KV cache central to the attention unit.  That expansion can impose a restrictive memory bottleneck on the LLM.  Already, supported context windows in SOTA systems have grown significantly ~\\\\cite{bib.bib11, bib.bib12, bib.bib13, bib.bib14}, underscoring the need for a solution.  One powerful remedy is quantization, wherein high-precision numbers are reduced to low-precision formats ~\\\\cite{bib.bib15, bib.bib16}.  In LLMs, this can be applied to the KV-cache tensors (e. g. , from BF16 to INT4) yielding substantial memory savings with minimal performance loss. \\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: \\n  10: This process is known as KV cache quantization.  Extensive work has been done in designing novel KV quantization frameworks, yet none so far have provided deep investigation into mixed-precision schemes, in particular those which focus on the bit allocations split between the Key and Value caches.  Instead, previous works have treated the bit allocation as a hyperparameter, seeing it as an object for optimization via grid search rather than taking a deeper dive into the properties of Keys and Values.  We provide further motivation for the study in the form of a full description of the current literature, which is detailed in Section. \\n  11: \\n  12: \\n  13: Therefore, there is a present need for a deep exploration into the inherent differences between the Key and the Value caches, as well as a change to the way that quantization is performed.  This study aims to fill this need by uncovering fundamental theoretical ideas to improve upon KV cache quantization methods.  A preview of these results is illustrated in Figure (left), showing that the spectral norms of the Keys consistently exceed those of the values.  Additionally, Figure (right) demonstrates that accuracy across four different models is notably higher for the K4V2 quantization configuration compared to the K2V4 configuration.  Our main contributions are summarized as follows:\\n  14: \\n  15: \\n  16: \\n  17: \u2022\\n  18: \\n  19: We prove that the expected values of the spectral norm and Frobenius norm are consistently higher for Key weight matrices compared to Value weight matrices (Key-Value Norm Disparity theorem), implying that Key matrices inherently carry more information.  We provide detailed empirical validation through observational studies on multiple LLMs. \\n  20: \\n  21: \u2022\\n  22: \\n  23: Building on the Key-Value Norm Disparity, we introduce the Key-Driven Quantization theorem, positing that assigning higher bit precision to Keys over Values significantly enhances quantization efficiency.  Specifically, this approach allows for greater precision reduction while maintaining minimal accuracy loss. \\n  24: \\n  25: \u2022\\n  26: \\n  27: We substantiate the Key-Driven Quantization theorem through two primary forms of evidence: (1) a theoretical analysis explicitly linking it to the previously established Key-Value Norm Disparity, and (2) comprehensive empirical evaluations involving multiple SOTA LLMs, three datasets, and two quantization frameworks. \\n  28: \\n  29: \\n  30: \\n  31: \\n  32: Section addresses gaps in the existing literature on KV cache quantization, followed by Section , which introduces the Key-Value Norm Disparity theorem and its supporting evidence.  Section presents the Key-Driven Quantization theorem along with its corresponding proof, and Section reports the empirical evaluation of both theorems.  Finally, Section summarizes the main contributions and discusses their limitations.\\n  33: \\n  34: \\n  35: 2 Related Work KV Quantization Background.\\n  36: Quantization frameworks can be categorized in several ways.  One way is the time at which the quantization is performed, which is grouped into training-time and post-training (PTQ) quantization techniques ~\\\\cite{bib.bib17}.  Training-time quantization frameworks can struggle with the usual costs of neural network training, including the dependence on labelled data and longer training times, but these frameworks can achieve more accurate performance due to targeting the weights or activations during the training process.  In contrast, post-training quantization techniques are the reverse, struggling with sometimes less accurate performance due to dealing with the values after the training has been completed but achieving lower computation overhead and no longer relying on labelled data which may not be available ~\\\\cite{bib.bib16}. \\n  37: \\n  38: \\n  39: There are several settings for PTQ: weight-only, weight-activation, and KV quantization.  Weight-only quantization focuses on the weights and achieves strong performance but can struggle with memory overhead ~\\\\cite{bib.bib18, bib.bib19, bib.bib20}.  Weight-activation quantization focuses on both the weights and the activations and avoids memory overhead but can struggle with achieving high accuracy ~\\\\cite{bib.bib21, bib.bib22, bib.bib23}.  In contrast, KV quantization offers the memory savings seen in weight-activation methods while also maintaining the performance of weight-only quantization ~\\\\cite{bib.bib24}.  This is due to the KV cache memory overhead inflation caused by longer sequences ~\\\\cite{bib.bib25}. \\n  40: \\n  41: \\n  42: KV quantization frameworks can be further categorized into three groups based on the exact quantization scheme being used for the keys and values: outlier redistribution, fixed-precision, and mixed-precision ~\\\\cite{bib.bib26}.  In outlier redistribution, the outliers in the cache are moved elsewhere or smoothed out.  Several outlier redistribution frameworks have been built to varying levels of success ~\\\\cite{bib.bib22, bib.bib20, bib.bib23}.  In fixed-precision, the same number of bits is used to quantize certain parts of the cache while in mixed-precision, different numbers of bits are used.  Fixed-precision frameworks have also been built to varying levels of success, though they all suffer from a similar problem of neglecting the inherent properties within the KV cache as well as the varying importance of tokens ~\\\\cite{bib.bib27, bib.bib28, bib.bib29}. \\n  43: \\n  44: \\n  45: More focus has been devoted to the third type of KV quantization framework, mixed-precision, but as yet, these works have not looked much into asymmetric allocation into keys and values ~\\\\cite{bib.bib30, bib.bib24, bib.bib31, bib.bib32, bib.bib33, bib.bib34, bib.bib35}.  KVQuant, for example, focuses on defining an outlier for each vector, such as channel or token, to achieve what the authors term dense-and-sparse quantization.  Only KVTuner, QAQ, and SKVQ discuss the asymmetric allocation in some detail, which is described below.\\n  46: \\n  47: \\n  48: 2 Related Work KV Quantization Gaps.\\n  49: As described above, extensive work has been done in designing new KV quantization frameworks, yet none so far have conducted deeper investigation into mixed-precision schemes.  In particular, no studies have focused on making a bit allocation split between the key matrix and the value matrix, nor have they provided a deep theoretical explanation for the inherent differences between the two matrices.  Only three studies to date have touched upon this area, with none providing explanations for potential differences between the key and value matrix importance. \\n  50: \\n  51: \\n  52: The closest study has been a KV quantization framework called KVTuner, which employs layerwise quantization based on the sensitivity of the layers to the KV cache quantization mode and precision pairs ~\\\\cite{bib.bib35}.  The study makes a brief mention of the difference in attention score errors and perplexity score errors, observing that precision pairs with more bits allocated for keys than for values achieves similar accuracy than for even-split pairs, such as K8V4 versus K8V8.  However, the study makes no further analysis into this observation, providing no reason for why this difference is observed.  In addition, the quantization approach does not use any underlying insight on this difference between key and values, instead opting for a straightforward grid search over a limited amount of precision pairs such as K8V4, K4V8, K4V2, and so on.  Therefore, this allocation split of bits is not the core focus of the framework, with the focus instead being on deploying a layerwise quantization scheme. \\n  53: \\n  54: \\n  55: Two other studies also touch upon the key-value difference, but like KVTuner, do not provide much depth into the difference. The quantization strategy achieves 2 bit key quantization and 1.5 bit value quantization, but the authors do not explore the possible reasons behind why this difference in bit allocation yielded such powerful results, instead arriving at this bit allocation via hyperparameter search. \\n  56: \\n  57: \\n  58: The other study is a KV quantization framework called QAQ, which uses the attention output to perform the key quantization and the self-attention output to perform the value quantization ~\\\\cite{bib.bib32}. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_ogp1c9VylDYQ6zrEomvBXKbU\", \"content\": \"\\n[Paper Details]\\nIdentifier: 2604.16883\\nIdentifier Type: arxiv\\n\\n==============================\\n   1: \\n   2: 1. Introduction\\n   3: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) are increasingly expected to process extended contexts, ranging from long textual histories to high-resolution images and videos~\\\\cite{bib.bib19, bib.bib18, bib.bib21, bib.bib20}.  However, long-context autoregressive decoding introduces a critical systems bottleneck: at each decoding step, the model must repeatedly load an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache for attention computation.  As the context length increases, this repeated fetching of the KV cache makes decoding increasingly memory-bound, thereby creating substantial pressure on memory bandwidth and incurring significant latency overhead on modern hardware~\\\\cite{bib.bib22, bib.bib23, bib.bib29}. \\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: A large body of recent work aims to alleviate this bottleneck through token eviction or KV-cache compression~\\\\cite{bib.bib17, bib.bib1, bib.bib28, bib.bib25}.  These approaches are effective in reducing memory footprint and decoding cost, but they primarily operate at the token or cache level.  Consequently, they may discard context that later becomes useful, and their token-level sparsity patterns do not naturally align with the execution granularity of Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), which makes it difficult to consistently translate algorithmic sparsity into hardware speedup~\\\\cite{bib.bib27}. \\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: Attention sinks have been widely observed in long-context decoding and are often associated with stabilization or anchor preservation~\\\\cite{bib.bib1, bib.bib30}.  Here, we revisit this phenomenon from a mechanistic perspective.  During decoding, initial tokens such as BOS in Llama models often attract a disproportionately large share of attention mass~\\\\cite{bib.bib1}.  Our analysis suggests that this behavior is not merely a byproduct of the architecture, but is instead related to an adaptive bypass pattern acquired during training.  Empirically, we find that the norm of the BOS value vector remains close to zero across layers, effectively acting as a numerical vacuum, while the BOS key remains geometrically separated from semantic tokens, making it a stable and easily reachable target.  This combination allows certain attention heads to route toward BOS and produce an approximately null update to the residual stream when additional contextual enrichment is unnecessary.  From this perspective, attention sinks provide a natural signal for identifying potentially idle heads during decoding. \\n  10: \\n  11: \\n  12: Motivated by this observation, we propose SinkRouter, a plug-and-play, training-free decoding framework that uses sink-aware signals to selectively bypass weakly contributing attention heads.  Rather than evicting tokens or compressing cached states, SinkRouter operates at the head level, reducing unnecessary KV-cache loading while preserving the retained context. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_E99cApFYAo9aWr1EVYQPtvrf\", \"content\": \"\\n[Paper Details]\\nIdentifier: 2606.06160\\nIdentifier Type: arxiv\\n\\n==============================\\n   1: \\n   2: 1 Introduction\\n   3: Decoder-only transformers trained with rotary position embeddings\\n   4: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib1} compute attention through inner products that,\\n   5: by construction, depend on the difference i\u2212ji-j of the two positions. \\n   6: A model trained under this design should be unable to distinguish a\\n   7: token at position 5050 from the same token at position 100100 except\\n   8: through its relations to other tokens.  RoPE-trained models make this\\n   9: distinction readily; their attention patterns carry traces of absolute\\n  10: position not predictable from relative offset alone\\n  11: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib2, bib.bib3}.  The relative encoding\\n  12: leaks though: our concern in this paper is where the leakage comes from and\\n  13: by what mechanism it arrives at the attention computations that\\n  14: consume it. \\n  15: \\n  16: \\n  17: A natural first guess identifies the attention sink as the locus. \\n  18: Sinks are the token that marks the start of the sequence that absorb a large share of attention from every query ~\\\\cite{bib.bib4, bib.bib5}, they are visited globally, appear early in the network, and\\n  19: from the outside have the appearance of aggregators.  We find that\\n  20: sinks carry no decodable content.  The positions with the highest\\n  21: attention magnitude have topic-probe accuracy at chance; the positions\\n  22: decodable above chance have attention magnitudes three orders of\\n  23: magnitude smaller.  The sink is a token-anchored feature: moving the\\n  24: BOS token from position 00 to position 88 moves the sink\\n  25: with it, and replacing BOS with a random uncommon token\\n  26: suppresses the sink entirely.  Sink-reading heads pass the identity of\\n  27: the sink token to downstream attention: in models that auto-prepend\\n  28: BOS this signal is constant across inputs, in Qwen it varies\\n  29: with whatever token sits at position 00. \\n  30: \\n  31: \\n  32: The leakage has two architectural sources.  The causal mask supplies\\n  33: one: its per-query softmax denominator depends on the absolute query\\n  34: position by construction, regardless of what the logits encode.  The\\n  35: residual stream supplies the other: position-varying activations flow\\n  36: into queries and keys, and RoPE rotation does not fully obscure them. \\n  37: We isolate the two components through ablations of the attention\\n  38: computation, and find both present in all three architectures we study,\\n  39: in architecturally specific balance. \\n  40: The residual-stream component itself traces to a single mechanism. \\n  41: Under causal attention, position 00 attends only to itself; the\\n  42: activation at position 00 at every layer is a deterministic function\\n  43: of the embedding of the token there.\\n  44: \\n  45: \\n  46: 2 Related Work Attention sinks\\n  47: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib4} identified attention sinks as a stable feature\\n  48: of decoder-only transformers and exploited them in StreamingLLM to\\n  49: maintain quality under context truncation.  ~\\\\cite{bib.bib5}\\n  50: characterized the training dynamics under which sinks emerge. \\n  51: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib6} analyzed sinks as a geometric reference frame\\n  52: for downstream attention.  Whether sinks function as information\\n  53: aggregators or as content-free stabilizers has remained ambiguous in\\n  54: the literature; our results support the latter reading and identify\\n  55: token-anchoring rather than position-anchoring as the empirical\\n  56: signature.\\n  57: \\n  58: \\n  59: 2 Related Work Positional encodings\\n  60: RoPE ~\\\\cite{bib.bib1} encodes position through relative offsets\\n  61: in the inner product, and has become the dominant choice in open-source\\n  62: language models.  The design property of\\n  63: Equation has nevertheless been shown to leak:\\n  64: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib2} demonstrated that the choice of positional\\n  65: encoding affects length-generalization in ways the relative-only design\\n  66: does not predict, and ~\\\\cite{bib.bib3} documented\\n  67: absolute-position structure in attention patterns of RoPE-trained\\n  68: models.  ALiBi ~\\\\cite{bib.bib7} and the NTK-/YaRN-style\\n  69: extensions ~\\\\cite{bib.bib8} modify position encoding to address\\n  70: length-generalization specifically.  Our work locates the leakage\\n  71: downstream of the inner product, in the softmax normalization rather\\n  72: than in RoPE itself.\\n  73: \\n  74: \\n  75: 2 Related Work Causal masking and mechanistic interpretation\\n  76: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib9} showed that decoder-only transformers\\n  77: trained without explicit positional encodings can still solve\\n  78: sequence tasks, attributing the residual position signal to the\\n  79: asymmetry the causal mask introduces.  Our work identifies the\\n  80: mechanism more precisely: the position-dependent cardinality of the\\n  81: per-query softmax denominator, isolated by the bidirectional\\n  82: ablation.  On the interpretability side, the targeted-ablation\\n  83: literature has localized many model behaviors to specific heads,\\n  84: circuits, or low-rank directions\\n  85: ~\\\\cite{bib.bib10, bib.bib11}.  The\\n  86: absolute-position structure we study resists this kind of\\n  87: localization across two separate intervention families, consistent\\n  88: with a mechanism that lives in the normalization rather than in any\\n  89: weight.\\n  90: \\n  91: \\n  92: 3 Background and the leakage metric\\n  93: RoPE applies a position-dependent rotation to queries and keys without\\n  94: modifying the residual stream from which they are derived.  For a head\\n  95: with head dimension dhd_{h} and unrotated query and key qm,kn\u2208\u211ddhq_{m},k_{n}\\\\in\\\\{R}^{d_{h}}, RoPE multiplies each by a block-diagonal orthogonal\\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__paper_search__get_paper_fulltext\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_0MAzjn7FOZhuXqTVtzroAYyd\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n   1: # Pinpointing Attention-Causal Communication in Language Models\\n   2: \\n   3: [NeurIPS Proceedings](/)\\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: \\n   7: \\n   8: Search\\n   9: \\n  10: # Pinpointing Attention-Causal Communication in Language Models\\n  11: \\n  12: Gabriel Franco, Mark Crovella\\n  13: \\n  14: [Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 Main Conference (NeurIPS 2025)](/paper_files/paper/2025/vol38-main-conference)\\n  15: Main Conference Track\\n  16: \\n  17: [Bibtex](/paper_files/paper/30265-/bibtex) [Paper](/paper_files/paper/2025/file/3486e35eb33b5463e25d00b765edf229-Paper-Conference.pdf) [Supplemental](/paper_files/paper/2025/file/3486e35eb33b5463e25d00b765edf229-Supplemental-Conference.zip)\\n  18: \\n  19: ## Abstract\\n  20: \\n  21: The attention mechanism plays a central role in the computations performed by transformer-based models, and understanding the reasons why heads attend to specific tokens can aid in interpretability of language models. Although considerable work has shown that models construct low-dimensional feature representations, little work has explicitly tied low-dimensional features to the attention mechanism itself. In this paper we work to bridge this gap by presenting methods for identifying *attention-causal communication*, meaning low-dimensional features that are written into and read from tokens, and that have a provable causal relationship to attention patterns. The starting point for our method is prior work [1-3] showing that model components make use of low dimensional communication channels that can be exposed by the singular vectors of QK matrices. Our contribution is to provide a rigorous and principled approach to finding those channels and isolating the attention-causal signals they contain. We show that by identifying those signals, we can perform prompt-specific circuit discovery in a single forward pass. Further, we show that signals can uncover unexplored mechanisms at work in the model, including a surprising degree of global coordination across attention heads.\\n  22: \\n  23: ## DOI\\n  24: \\n  25: [10.52202/085713-1239](https://doi.org/10.52202/085713-1239)\\n  26: \\n  27:   \\n  28: \\n  29: #### Name Change Policy\\n  30: \\n  31: \u00d7\\n  32: \\n  33: Requests for name changes in the electronic proceedings will be accepted with no questions asked. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_iGT9dvlYgtkF7bipwa9gKbBk\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n   1: # [2604.14722] A Mechanistic Account of Attention Sinks in GPT-2: One Circuit, Broader Implications for Mitigation\\n   2: \\n   3: [Skip to main content](#content)\\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: [![archive](/static/base/1.0.1/images/arxiv-logo-primary-light.svg)](https://arxiv.org/)\\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: \\n  10: \\n  11: \\n  12: \\n  13: \\n  14: [Search](https://arxiv.org/search)\\n  15: [Submit](https://arxiv.org/user/create)\\n  16: [Donate](https://info.arxiv.org/about/donate.html)\\n  17: \\n  18: [Log in](https://arxiv.org/login)\\n  19: \\n  20: Search arXiv\\n  21: \\n  22: Press Enter to search \u00b7 [Advanced search](https://arxiv.org/search/advanced)\\n  23: \\n  24: # Computer Science > Machine Learning\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2604.14722** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 16 Apr 2026]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:A Mechanistic Account of Attention Sinks in GPT-2: One Circuit, Broader Implications for Mitigation\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Yuval Ran-Milo](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Ran-Milo,+Y), [Hila Ofek](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Ofek,+H), [Shahar Mendel](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Mendel,+S)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled A Mechanistic Account of Attention Sinks in GPT-2: One Circuit, Broader Implications for Mitigation, by Yuval Ran-Milo and 2 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2604.14722)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.14722v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:Transformers commonly exhibit an attention sink: disproportionately high attention to the first position. We study this behavior in GPT-2-style models with learned query biases and absolute positional embeddings. Combining structural analysis with causal interventions, validated across natural-language, mathematical, and code inputs, we find that the sink arises from the interaction among (i) a learned query bias, (ii) the first-layer MLP transformation of the positional encoding, and (iii) structure in the key projection. Crucially, each component we identify is individually dispensable: architectures omitting each of them robustly exhibit sinks. This indicates that attention sinks may arise through distinct circuits across architectures. These findings inform mitigation of sinks, and motivate broader investigation into why sinks emerge.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Comments: | 9 pages, 8 figures |\\n  43: | Subjects: | Machine Learning (cs.LG) |\\n  44: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2604.14722](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14722) [cs.LG] |\\n  45: |  | (or  [arXiv:2604.14722v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14722v1) [cs.LG] for this version) |\\n  46: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.14722> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  47: \\n  48: ## Submission history\\n  49: \\n  50: From: Yuval Ran-Milo [[view email](/show-email/74874532/2604.14722)]   \\n  51:  **[v1]**\\n  52: Thu, 16 Apr 2026 07:32:37 UTC (529 KB)\\n  53: \\n  54: Full-text links:\\n  55: \\n  56: ## Access Paper:\\n  57: \\n  58: View a PDF of the paper titled A Mechanistic Account of Attention Sinks in GPT-2: One Circuit, Broader Implications for Mitigation, by Yuval Ran-Milo and 2 other authors\\n  59: \\n  60: * [View PDF](/pdf/2604.14722)\\n  61: * [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.14722v1)\\n  62: * [TeX Source](/src/2604.14722)\\n  63: \\n  64: [![license icon](https://arxiv.org/icons/licenses/by-4.0.png)\\n  65: view license](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ \\\"Rights to this article\\\")\\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_oOgLt96xMuC6AUDZ7asMZhuq\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n   1: # [2606.08105] A Unifying View of Attention Sinks: From Mechanisms to Architectural Interventions\\n   2: \\n   3: [Skip to main content](#content)\\n   4: \\n   5: \\n   6: [![archive](/static/base/1.0.1/images/arxiv-logo-primary-light.svg)](https://arxiv.org/)\\n   7: \\n   8: \\n   9: \\n  10: \\n  11: \\n  12: \\n  13: \\n  14: [Search](https://arxiv.org/search)\\n  15: [Submit](https://arxiv.org/user/create)\\n  16: [Donate](https://info.arxiv.org/about/donate.html)\\n  17: \\n  18: [Log in](https://arxiv.org/login)\\n  19: \\n  20: Search arXiv\\n  21: \\n  22: Press Enter to search \u00b7 [Advanced search](https://arxiv.org/search/advanced)\\n  23: \\n  24: # Computer Science > Machine Learning\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2606.08105** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 6 Jun 2026 ([v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08105v1)), last revised 5 Oct 2026 (this version, v2)]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:A Unifying View of Attention Sinks: From Mechanisms to Architectural Interventions\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Lukas Fesser\\\\*](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Fesser*,+L), [Mozes Jacobs\\\\*](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Jacobs*,+M), [Thomas Fel\\\\*](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Fel*,+T), [Andy Keller](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Keller,+A), [Sham Kakade](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Kakade,+S)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled A Unifying View of Attention Sinks: From Mechanisms to Architectural Interventions, by Lukas Fesser\\\\* and 4 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2606.08105)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.08105v2)\\n  38: > Abstract:When attention concentrates on a single token, a sink, what is the model actually computing? Attention sinks are ubiquitous in softmax transformers, yet this shared visual signature can hide fundamentally different algorithms. We show that visually similar sink patterns can reflect two distinct mechanisms: (i) adaptive nop, where a head suppresses its update by routing to a null token, and (ii) broadcast, where a sink aggregates and redistributes global information. Each mechanism leaves distinct traces (nop-sinks exhibit negligible value norms; broadcast sinks induce low-rank outputs), which we formalize on synthetic tasks and use to derive practical diagnostics. Applied to pretrained vision transformers, these diagnostics reveal that both mechanisms exist at scale: sinks transition from CLS in early layers to patches in deeper layers and concentrate in specialized heads. Causal interventions further connect these signatures to near-null suppression and shared residual contributions. We then use architectural interventions to show how these computations can be reorganized: gating eliminates detected nop-like sinks but increases broadcast-like sinks, registers relocate rather than remove sink computation, and our position-free global pathway provides an explicit route for shared communication that reduces the broadcast-like sinks induced by gating. On dense probes, combining gating with the global pathway gives the strongest results among the tested variants, despite retaining some broadcast-like sinks. Overall, we find that the same attention pattern can reflect two very different computations, and that effective intervention depends not only on identifying the computation, but also on providing architectural alternatives through which the model can reorganize it.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Subjects: | Machine Learning (cs.LG) |\\n  43: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2606.08105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08105) [cs.LG] |\\n  44: |  | (or  [arXiv:2606.08105v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08105v2) [cs.LG] for this version) |\\n  45: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.08105> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  46: \\n  47: ## Submission history\\n  48: \\n  49: From: Lukas Fesser [[view email](/show-email/c0ccca27/2606.08105)]   \\n  50:  **[[v1]](/abs/2606.08105v1)**\\n  51: Sat, 6 Jun 2026 11:10:54 UTC (15,566 KB)  \\n  52: **[v2]**\\n  53: Mon, 5 Oct 2026 16:07:49 UTC (12,667 KB)\\n  54: \\n  55: Full-text links:\\n  56: \\n  57: ## Access Paper:\\n  58: \\n  59: View a PDF of the paper titled A Unifying View of Attention Sinks: From Mechanisms to Architectural Interventions, by Lukas Fesser\\\\* and 4 other authors\\n  60: \\n  61: * [View PDF](/pdf/2606.08105)\\n  62: * [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.08105v2)\\n  63: * [TeX Source](/src/2606.08105)\\n  64: \\n  65: [![license icon](https://arxiv.org/icons/licenses/by-4.0.png)\\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

Attention Rows as Compositional Data\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Marios Papamichalis](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Papamichalis,+M), [Regina Ruane](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Ruane,+R)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled Which Question Is Your Attention Metric Answering? Attention Rows as Compositional Data, by Marios Papamichalis and 1 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2608.14712)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.14712v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:Each row of a transformer's attention matrix is a probability distribution over tokens, and in trained models most of that probability lands on a single \\\\emph{sink} token, usually the first. Standard tools for comparing attention rows (cosine similarity, Jensen--Shannon divergence, Shannon entropy) therefore hinge on a choice papers rarely report: keep the sink, or drop it and renormalize. This choice can reverse conclusions. On ten pretrained models from five families, 17--47% of verdicts about which of two heads is more similar flip with the convention, and the most prominent structure in a standard BERT head-clustering pipeline is an artifact of it. The reason is that one-number summaries mix two questions: how much attention the sink takes, and how the rest is divided among the content tokens. Treating rows as compositional data separates them exactly: the Aitchison distance splits orthogonally into a sink term and a content term, entropy splits by an exact identity, and the content distance is characterized by invariances the transformer itself possesses. The separation matters in practice: most measured entropy collapse during training is the sink growing, not attention sharpening (30% of the drop at 70M parameters, 95% at 1B, 79% at 1.4B), and pruning heads with the wrong channel can inflate perplexity more than a hundredfold. We map where each convention is safe, test a frozen out-of-sample predictor (one confirmation, one abstention, one failure), and release code regenerating every number.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Comments: | Preprint under submission |\\n  43: | Subjects: | Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST) |\\n  44: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2608.14712](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14712) [cs.CL] |\\n  45: |  | (or  [arXiv:2608.14712v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14712v1) [cs.CL] for this version) |\\n  46: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.14712> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  47: \\n  48: ## Submission history\\n  49: \\n  50: From: Marios Papamichalis Dr [[view email](/show-email/5574e1c5/2608.14712)]   \\n  51:  **[v1]**\\n  52: Tue, 11 Aug 2026 16:44:01 UTC (565 KB)\\n  53: \\n  54: Full-text links:\\n  55: \\n  56: ## Access Paper:\\n  57: \\n  58: View a PDF of the paper titled Which Question Is Your Attention Metric Answering?
