Inputs: Pythia 410M/1B first, optional current 1-3B rotary GQA model after config audit; cache capacities 256/512, first-N and detected sinks. Compare K16/V16, K16/V4, K4/V16, K4/V4 for protected groups while fixing nonsink quantizers; use published asymmetric K-channel/V-token axes, scales and zero-point accounting. Freeze group selection on development documents; test 200 independent held-out streams, including code/prose shifts and 64-token post-eviction windows. Compare KVSink, SubKV, first-N, random and recent-token allocation at equal actual bytes; count residual buffers and metadata. At declared boundaries compare a 2-by-2 design: original versus fresh-session anchor states, crossed with reused versus fresh-session-recomputed suffix states. Mixed-state arms are diagnostic interventions, not production reset policies. Within each suffix-state arm hold suffix tensors and cache-local position convention identical; regenerate pre-RoPE keys or correctly inverse/reapply rotation and assert equality for the no-op control. All states come from the same model revision and same isolated session. Primary endpoint is positive excess-NLL area over the first 64 post-boundary tokens relative to that arm's unchanged-anchor control; report peak loss and recovery separately. Use 200 held-out stream boundaries with document-cluster bootstrap, domain strata, a recomputation control and matched nonsink patches. Go: effect exceeds a development-fixed practical threshold with 95% interval excluding zero and survives position/backend checks; otherwise attribute to implementation or reject. No claim of recalling evicted facts; later states may retain indirect traces. Deliverable: reproducible boundary audit and reset compatibility checklist, not an infinite-memory mechanism.\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"next_action\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"Follow-up session: build pre-/post-RoPE cache consistency tests, implement isolated-session factorial diagnostic arms, choose the practical threshold on development streams, then release 64-token boundary loss traces, recovery estimates and a position-correct reset checklist.\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"references\\\\\\\":[\\\\\\\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07282\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16883\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06160\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\"https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09085\\\\\\\"],\\\\\\\"gates\\\\\\\":{\\\\\\\"novelty\\\\\\\":true,\\\\\\\"gap\\\\\\\":true,\\\\\\\"feasibility\\\\\\\":true,\\\\\\\"references\\\\\\\":true}}]}\\\\n\\\"}\"}}], \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

This phenomenon has been widely adopted in applications such as streaming/long context generation, KV cache optimization, inference acceleration, model quantization, and others. Despite its widespread use, a deep understanding of attention sink in LMs is still lacking. In this work, we first demonstrate that attention sinks exist universally in LMs with various inputs, even in small models. Furthermore, attention sink is observed to emerge during the LM pre-training, motivating us to investigate how optimization, data distribution, loss function, and model architecture in LM pre-training influence its emergence. We highlight that attention sink emerges after effective optimization on sufficient training data. The sink position is highly correlated with the loss function and data distribution. Most importantly, we find that attention sink acts more like key biases, storing extra attention scores, which could be non-informative and not contribute to the value computation. We also observe that this phenomenon (at least partially) stems from tokens' inner dependence on attention scores as a result of softmax normalization. After relaxing such dependence by replacing softmax attention with other attention operations, such as sigmoid attention without normalization, attention sinks do not emerge in LMs up to 1B parameters. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_qrVhOaqJyLJ9b7XhvZEni0BY\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Computation and Language\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2309.17453** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 29 Sep 2023 ([v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453v1)), last revised 7 Apr 2024 (this version, v4)]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Guangxuan Xiao](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Xiao,+G), [Yuandong Tian](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Tian,+Y), [Beidi Chen](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Chen,+B), [Song Han](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Han,+S), [Mike Lewis](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Lewis,+M)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks, by Guangxuan Xiao and 4 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2309.17453)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.17453v4)\\n  38: > Abstract:Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in streaming applications such as multi-round dialogue, where long interactions are expected, is urgently needed but poses two major challenges. Firstly, during the decoding stage, caching previous tokens' Key and Value states (KV) consumes extensive memory. Secondly, popular LLMs cannot generalize to longer texts than the training sequence length. Window attention, where only the most recent KVs are cached, is a natural approach -- but we show that it fails when the text length surpasses the cache size. We observe an interesting phenomenon, namely attention sink, that keeping the KV of initial tokens will largely recover the performance of window attention. In this paper, we first demonstrate that the emergence of attention sink is due to the strong attention scores towards initial tokens as a \\\"sink\\\" even if they are not semantically important. Based on the above analysis, we introduce StreamingLLM, an efficient framework that enables LLMs trained with a finite length attention window to generalize to infinite sequence lengths without any fine-tuning. We show that StreamingLLM can enable Llama-2, MPT, Falcon, and Pythia to perform stable and efficient language modeling with up to 4 million tokens and more. In addition, we discover that adding a placeholder token as a dedicated attention sink during pre-training can further improve streaming deployment. In streaming settings, StreamingLLM outperforms the sliding window recomputation baseline by up to 22.2x speedup. Code and datasets are provided at [this https URL](https://github.com/mit-han-lab/streaming-llm).\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Comments: | ICLR 2024 |\\n  43: | Subjects: | Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) |\\n  44: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2309.17453](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453) [cs.CL] |\\n  45: |  | (or  [arXiv:2309.17453v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453v4) [cs.CL] for this version) |\\n  46: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2309.17453> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  47: \\n  48: ## Submission history\\n  49: \\n  50: From: Guangxuan Xiao [[view email](/show-email/a1f20a90/2309.17453)]   \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_VFtiVPEH0AEkH6EcdiFMMf6Y\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Computation and Language\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2402.02750** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 5 Feb 2024 ([v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02750v1)), last revised 25 Jul 2024 (this version, v2)]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Zirui Liu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Liu,+Z), [Jiayi Yuan](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Yuan,+J), [Hongye Jin](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Jin,+H), [Shaochen Zhong](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zhong,+S), [Zhaozhuo Xu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Xu,+Z), [Vladimir Braverman](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Braverman,+V), [Beidi Chen](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Chen,+B), [Xia Hu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Hu,+X)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache, by Zirui Liu and 7 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2402.02750)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.02750v2)\\n  38: > Abstract:Efficiently serving large language models (LLMs) requires batching of many requests to reduce the cost per request. Yet, with larger batch sizes and longer context lengths, the key-value (KV) cache, which stores attention keys and values to avoid re-computations, significantly increases memory demands and becomes the new bottleneck in speed and memory usage. Additionally, the loading of the KV cache causes the computational core to be idle, which limits the inference speed. A straightforward and effective solution to reduce KV cache size is quantization, which decreases the total bytes taken by KV cache. However, there is a lack of in-depth studies that explore the element distribution of KV cache to understand the hardness and limitation of KV cache quantization. To fill the gap, we conducted a comprehensive study on the element distribution in KV cache of popular LLMs. Our findings indicate that the key cache should be quantized per-channel, i.e., group elements along the channel dimension and quantize them together. In contrast, the value cache should be quantized per-token. From this analysis, we developed a tuning-free 2bit KV cache quantization algorithm named KIVI. With hardware-friendly implementation, KIVI can enable Llama, Falcon, and Mistral models to maintain almost the same quality while using $\\\\mathbf{2.6\\\\times}$ less peak memory (including model weight). This reduction in memory usage enables up to $\\\\mathbf{4\\\\times}$ larger batch size, bringing $\\\\mathbf{2.35\\\\times \\\\sim 3.47\\\\times}$ throughput on real LLM inference workload. The source code is available at [this https URL](https://github.com/jy-yuan/KIVI).\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Comments: | ICML2024 |\\n  43: | Subjects: | Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Performance (cs.PF) |\\n  44: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2402.02750](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02750) [cs.CL] |\\n  45: |  | (or  [arXiv:2402.02750v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02750v2) [cs.CL] for this version) |\\n  46: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2402.02750> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  47: | Related DOI: | <https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.28167.37282>  Focus to learn more  DOI(s) linking to related resources |\\n  48: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_v71tPDBxwO6JyuJUvUXvMwM4\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Machine Learning\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2405.06219** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 10 May 2024 ([v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06219v1)), last revised 12 Nov 2024 (this version, v3)]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:SKVQ: Sliding-window Key and Value Cache Quantization for Large Language Models\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Haojie Duanmu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Duanmu,+H), [Zhihang Yuan](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Yuan,+Z), [Xiuhong Li](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Li,+X), [Jiangfei Duan](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Duan,+J), [Xingcheng Zhang](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zhang,+X), [Dahua Lin](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Lin,+D)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled SKVQ: Sliding-window Key and Value Cache Quantization for Large Language Models, by Haojie Duanmu and 5 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2405.06219)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.06219v3)\\n  38: > Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) can now handle longer sequences of tokens, enabling complex tasks like book understanding and generating lengthy novels. However, the key-value (KV) cache required for LLMs consumes substantial memory as context length increasing, becoming the bottleneck for deployment. In this paper, we present a strategy called SKVQ, which stands for sliding-window KV cache quantization, to address the issue of extremely low bitwidth KV cache quantization. To achieve this, SKVQ rearranges the channels of the KV cache in order to improve the similarity of channels in quantization groups, and applies clipped dynamic quantization at the group level. Additionally, SKVQ ensures that the most recent window tokens in the KV cache are preserved with high precision. This helps maintain the accuracy of a small but important portion of the KV [this http URL](http://cache.SKVQ) achieves high compression ratios while maintaining accuracy. Our evaluation on LLMs demonstrates that SKVQ surpasses previous quantization approaches, allowing for quantization of the KV cache to 2-bit keys and 1.5-bit values with minimal loss of accuracy. With SKVQ, it is possible to process context lengths of up to 1M on an 80GB memory GPU for a 7b model and up to 7 times faster decoding.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Subjects: | Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL) |\\n  43: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2405.06219](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06219) [cs.LG] |\\n  44: |  | (or  [arXiv:2405.06219v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06219v3) [cs.LG] for this version) |\\n  45: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.06219> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  46: \\n  47: ## Submission history\\n  48: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_ngSVAnQnGSn6QlgAjfktgYGv\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Computation and Language\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2609.07282** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 7 Sep 2026]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:Separating Stream Stability from Long-Term Recall in Language Models\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Peipei Cao](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Cao,+P), [Xin Zhang](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zhang,+X), [Jie Tang](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Tang,+J), [Xiao Li](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Li,+X), [Siying Li](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Li,+S), [Qing Pei](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Pei,+Q)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled Separating Stream Stability from Long-Term Recall in Language Models, by Peipei Cao and 5 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2609.07282)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.07282v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:Methods for streaming language models are often discussed alongside long-context and memory systems, although they solve different problems. An attention sink can stabilize autoregressive generation over an indefinitely long stream while the model remains unable to use content that has left its recent-token cache. We argue that this distinction should be explicit in system claims and evaluation. We introduce three horizons: the stability horizon, over which predictive behavior remains well behaved; the access horizon, over which past content can still causally affect the output; and the utility horizon, over which a task retains acceptable performance. We show constructively that the stability horizon can be infinite while the access and utility horizons are finite. We then propose ThreeH, an evaluation contract that measures all three horizons under a common state and compute budget. Applying the framework to attention-sink streaming clarifies its strength, constant-memory, stable generation, without treating anchor tokens as semantic memory. The framework exposes roles for cache policies, recurrent state, retrieval, and external memory. Experiments on 128K-token streams, delayed binding recall, and delayed decisions show that attention sinks preserve local modeling but not content beyond the active cache; recurrent and retrieval state extend the semantic horizon.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Subjects: | Computation and Language (cs.CL) |\\n  43: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2609.07282](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07282) [cs.CL] |\\n  44: |  | (or  [arXiv:2609.07282v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07282v1) [cs.CL] for this version) |\\n  45: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.07282> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite (pending registration) |\\n  46: \\n  47: ## Submission history\\n  48: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_XYvpuNMc35e9BsfXd9Ueimlw\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Machine Learning\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2604.16883** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 18 Apr 2026]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:SinkRouter: Sink-Aware Routing for Efficient Long-Context Decoding in Large Language and Multimodal Models\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Junnan Liu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Liu,+J), [Xinyan Liu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Liu,+X), [Peifeng Gao](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Gao,+P), [Zhaobo Qi](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Qi,+Z), [Beichen Zhang](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zhang,+B), [Weigang Zhang](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zhang,+W), [Antoni Bert Chen](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Chen,+A+B)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled SinkRouter: Sink-Aware Routing for Efficient Long-Context Decoding in Large Language and Multimodal Models, by Junnan Liu and 5 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2604.16883)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.16883v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:In long-context decoding for LLMs and LMMs, attention becomes increasingly memory-bound because each decoding step must load a large amount of KV-cache data from GPU memory. Existing acceleration strategies often trade efficiency for accuracy by relying on heuristic pruning that may discard useful information. At a deeper level, they also tend to indiscriminately preserve all high-scoring tokens, treat early tokens as indispensable anchors, or rely on heuristic head routing, reflecting an insufficient mechanistic understanding of the attention sink phenomenon. In this paper, we show that the attention sink phenomenon corresponds to a stable, reachable, and error-controllable fixed point constructed during training. Based on this insight, we propose SinkRouter, a training-free selective routing framework that detects the sink signal and skips computations that would otherwise produce near-zero output. To translate this mechanism into real-world acceleration, we develop a hardware-aware Triton kernel with block-level branching and Split-K parallelism. We conduct extensive evaluations on a diverse suite of long-context benchmarks, including LongBench, InfiniteBench, CVBench, MileBench, and MMVP, using both text-only and multimodal backbones such as Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Yi-9B-200K, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and LLaVA-1.5-13B. Across these settings, SinkRouter consistently improves decoding efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy, and reaches 2.03x speedup with a 512K context.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Subjects: | Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) |\\n  43: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2604.16883](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16883) [cs.LG] |\\n  44: |  | (or  [arXiv:2604.16883v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16883v1) [cs.LG] for this version) |\\n  45: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.16883> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  46: \\n  47: ## Submission history\\n  48: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_19YINAGOJbQxXLhXu3GHooT7\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Machine Learning\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2603.17771** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 18 Mar 2026 ([v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17771v1)), last revised 6 May 2026 (this version, v2)]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:Attention Sinks Induce Gradient Sinks: Massive Activations as Gradient Regulators in Transformers\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Yihong Chen](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Chen,+Y), [Zhouchen Lin](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Lin,+Z), [Quanming Yao](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Yao,+Q)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled Attention Sinks Induce Gradient Sinks: Massive Activations as Gradient Regulators in Transformers, by Yihong Chen and 2 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2603.17771)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.17771v2)\\n  38: > Abstract:Attention sinks and massive activations are recurring and closely related phenomena in Transformer models. Existing explanations have largely focused on the forward pass, yet in pre-norm Transformers, large residual-stream norms play only an indirect forward role because sublayers operate on normalized inputs. We study this relationship from the perspective of backpropagation. Empirically and theoretically, we show that under causal masking, attention sinks can induce pronounced gradient concentration, which we term gradient sinks. Since the RMSNorm Jacobian attenuates gradients roughly in inverse proportion to input norm, massive activations can be understood as adaptive regulators of this localized gradient pressure during training. This interpretation predicts that attenuating sink-induced gradients should weaken massive activations. We test this prediction with V-scale, a modification that adjusts backpropagated gradients on the value path. In V-scale models, attention sinks are preserved, whereas massive activations are suppressed. These results identify gradient sinks as a backward-pass counterpart of attention sinks, and massive activations as an adaptive RMSNorm-mediated response that attenuates the resulting localized training pressure. Our code is available at [this https URL](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GradientSinkCode-B309).\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Comments: | 29 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables |\\n  43: | Subjects: | Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) |\\n  44: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2603.17771](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17771) [cs.LG] |\\n  45: |  | (or  [arXiv:2603.17771v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17771v2) [cs.LG] for this version) |\\n  46: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.17771> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  47: \\n  48: ## Submission history\\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_h9nif45hAhwe25vhG5b8iXNi\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2606.06160** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 4 Jun 2026]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:Where does Absolute Position come from in decoder-only Transformers?\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Valeria Ruscio](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Ruscio,+V), [Umberto Nanni](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Nanni,+U), [Fabrizio Silvestri](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Silvestri,+F)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled Where does Absolute Position come from in decoder-only Transformers?, by Valeria Ruscio and 2 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2606.06160)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.06160v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:RoPE-trained transformers distinguish absolute position in their attention patterns, even though RoPE encodes only relative offsets in the inner product. We trace this leakage to two architectural components, The causal mask is responsible for the first: its per-query softmax denominator depends on the absolute query position by construction. The residual stream supplies the second. Under causal attention the activation at position $0$ attends only to itself and runs as a closed dynamical system from the embedding of the token at that position; downstream attention reads this trajectory through sink-reading heads. Both components appear in all three architectures we study, in architecturally specific balance: NTK scaling suppresses the residual-stream component, sliding-window attention allows it to accumulate with depth, and standard RoPE sits between. Replacing the \\\\texttt{BOS} embedding before the forward pass removes $40\\\\%$ of the residual-stream component at early queries. Attention sinks are token-anchored stabilizers that pass forward a deterministic fingerprint of the token at position $0$, constant across inputs when that token is the auto-prepended \\\\texttt{BOS} and varying with it otherwise.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Subjects: | Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL) |\\n  43: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2606.06160](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06160) [cs.AI] |\\n  44: |  | (or  [arXiv:2606.06160v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06160v1) [cs.AI] for this version) |\\n  45: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.06160> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  46: \\n  47: ## Submission history\\n  48: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

{"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_LYrOPVLCFNxkKnrMKiLYhtJX\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Computation and Language\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2609.09085** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 8 Sep 2026]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:It's Not RoPE that Creates Sinks: The Role of Self-Concentration and Value-Non-Mixing in Attention\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Raito Kiya](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Kiya,+R), [Satoki Ohashi](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Ohashi,+S), [Kosuke Sato](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Sato,+K), [Go Kamoda](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Kamoda,+G), [Ryosuke Takahashi](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Takahashi,+R), [Yuji Yamamoto](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Yamamoto,+Y), [Daiki Shiono](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Shiono,+D), [Keisuke Sakaguchi](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Sakaguchi,+K), [Goro Kobayashi](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Kobayashi,+G)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled It's Not RoPE that Creates Sinks: The Role of Self-Concentration and Value-Non-Mixing in Attention, by Raito Kiya and 8 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2609.09085)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.09085v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit \\\"Attention Sink\\\" (AS) and the accompanying \\\"Massive Activations\\\" (MAs) at the initial position of a sequence. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_xMsg7pFMAhBFRkl30C9QTIU5\", \"content\": \"{\\\"type\\\": \\\"text\\\", \\\"file\\\": {\\\"filePath\\\": \\\"/home/novix/.claude_data/skills/markdown-mermaid-writing/references/mermaid_style_guide.md\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"<!-- Source: https://github.com/SuperiorByteWorks-LLC/agent-project | License: Apache-2.0 | Author: Clayton Young / Superior Byte Works, LLC (Boreal Bytes) -->\\\\n\\\\n# Mermaid Diagram Style Guide\\\\n\\\\n> **For AI agents:** Read this file for all core styling rules. Then use the [diagram selection table](#choosing-the-right-diagram) to pick the right type and follow its link \u2014 each type has its own file with a production-quality exemplar, tips, and a copy-paste template.\\\\n>\\\\n> **For humans:** This guide + the linked diagram files ensure every Mermaid diagram in your repo is accessible, professional, and renders cleanly in GitHub light and dark modes. Reference it from your `AGENTS.md` or contributing guide.\\\\n\\\\n**Target platform:** GitHub Markdown (Issues, PRs, Discussions, Wikis, `.md` files)\\\\n**Design goal:** Minimal professional styling that renders beautifully in both GitHub light and dark modes, is accessible to screen readers, and communicates clearly with zero visual noise.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Quick Start for Agents\\\\n\\\\n1. **Pick the diagram type** \u2192 [Selection table](#choosing-the-right-diagram)\\\\n2. **Open that type's file** \u2192 Copy the template, fill in your content\\\\n3. **Apply styling from this file** \u2192 Emoji from [approved set](#approved-emoji-set), colors from [approved palette](#github-compatible-color-classes)\\\\n4. **Add accessibility** \u2192 `accTitle` + `accDescr` (or italic Markdown paragraph for unsupported types)\\\\n5. **Verify** \u2192 Renders in light mode, dark mode, and screen reader\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Core Principles\\\\n\\\\n| #   | Principle                      | Rule                                                                                                   |\\\\n| --- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\\\\n| 1   | **Clarity at every scale**     | Simple diagrams stay flat. Complex ones use subgraphs. Very complex ones split into overview + detail. |\\\\n| 2   | **Accessibility always**       | Every diagram gets `accTitle` + `accDescr`. No exceptions.                                             |\\\\n| 3   | **Theme neutral**              | No `%%{init}` theme directives. No inline `style`. Let GitHub auto-theme.                              |\\\\n| 4   | **Semantic clarity**           | `snake_case` node IDs that match labels. Active voice. Sentence case.                                  |\\\\n| 5   | **Consistent styling**         | Same emoji = same meaning everywhere. Same shapes = same semantics.                                    |\\\\n| 6   | **Minimal professional flair** | A touch of emoji + strategic bold + optional `classDef` \u2014 never more.                                  |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Accessibility Requirements\\\\n\\\\n**Every diagram MUST include both `accTitle` and `accDescr`:**\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\naccTitle: Short Name 3-8 Words\\\\naccDescr: One or two sentences explaining what this diagram shows and what insight the reader gains from it\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n- `accTitle` \u2014 3\u20138 words, plain text, names the diagram\\\\n- `accDescr` \u2014 1\u20132 sentences on a **single line** (GitHub limitation), explains purpose and key structure\\\\n\\\\n**Diagram types that do NOT support `accTitle`/`accDescr`:** Mindmap, Timeline, Quadrant, Sankey, XY Chart, Block, Kanban, Packet, Architecture, Radar, Treemap. For these, place a descriptive _italic_ Markdown paragraph directly above the code block as the accessible description.\\\\n\\\\n> **ZenUML note:** ZenUML requires an external plugin and may not render on GitHub. Prefer standard `sequenceDiagram` syntax.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Theme Configuration\\\\n\\\\n### \u2705 Do: No theme directive (GitHub auto-detects)\\\\n\\\\n```mermaid\\\\nflowchart LR\\\\n    accTitle: Secure API Request Flow\\\\n    accDescr: Three-step API request from authentication through processing to response\\\\n\\\\n    auth[\ud83d\udd10 Authenticate] --> process[\u2699\ufe0f Process request] --> respond[\ud83d\udce4 Return response]\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### \u274c Don't: Inline styles or custom themes\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\n%% BAD \u2014 breaks dark mode\\\\nstyle A fill:#e8f5e9\\\\n%%{init: {'theme':'base'}}%%\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Approved Emoji Set\\\\n\\\\nOne emoji per node, at the start of the label. Same emoji = same meaning across all diagrams in a project.\\\\n\\\\n### Systems & Infrastructure\\\\n\\\\n| Emoji | Meaning                           | Example                   |\\\\n| ----- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------- |\\\\n| \u2601\ufe0f    | Cloud / platform / hosted service | `[\u2601\ufe0f AWS Lambda]`         |\\\\n| \ud83c\udf10    | Network / web / connectivity      | `[\ud83c\udf10 API gateway]`        |\\\\n| \ud83d\udda5\ufe0f    | Server / compute / machine        | `[\ud83d\udda5\ufe0f Application server]` |\\\\n| \ud83d\udcbe    | Storage / database / persistence  | `[\ud83d\udcbe PostgreSQL]`         |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd0c    | Integration / plugin / connector  | `[\ud83d\udd0c Webhook handler]`    |\\\\n\\\\n### Processes & Actions\\\\n\\\\n| Emoji | Meaning                          | Example                   |\\\\n| ----- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------- |\\\\n| \u2699\ufe0f    | Process / configuration / engine | `[\u2699\ufe0f Build pipeline]`     |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd04    | Cycle / sync / recurring process | `[\ud83d\udd04 Retry loop]`         |\\\\n| \ud83d\ude80    | Deploy / launch / release        | `[\ud83d\ude80 Ship to production]` |\\\\n| \u26a1    | Fast action / trigger / event    | `[\u26a1 Webhook fired]`      |\\\\n| \ud83d\udce6    | Package / artifact / bundle      | `[\ud83d\udce6 Docker image]`       |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd27    | Tool / utility / maintenance     | `[\ud83d\udd27 Migration script]`   |\\\\n| \u23f0    | Scheduled / cron / time-based    | `[\u23f0 Nightly job]`        |\\\\n\\\\n### People & Roles\\\\n\\\\n| Emoji | Meaning                      | Example              |\\\\n| ----- | ---------------------------- | -------------------- |\\\\n| \ud83d\udc64    | User / person / actor        | `[\ud83d\udc64 End user]`      |\\\\n| \ud83d\udc65    | Team / group / organization  | `[\ud83d\udc65 Platform team]` |\\\\n| \ud83e\udd16    | Bot / agent / automation     | `[\ud83e\udd16 CI bot]`        |\\\\n| \ud83e\udde0    | Intelligence / decision / AI | `[\ud83e\udde0 ML classifier]` |\\\\n\\\\n### Status & Outcomes\\\\n\\\\n| Emoji | Meaning                         | Example                |\\\\n| ----- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------- |\\\\n| \u2705    | Success / approved / complete   | `[\u2705 Tests passed]`    |\\\\n| \u274c    | Failure / blocked / rejected    | `[\u274c Build failed]`    |\\\\n| \u26a0\ufe0f    | Warning / caution / risk        | `[\u26a0\ufe0f Rate limited]`    |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd12    | Locked / restricted / protected | `[\ud83d\udd12 Requires admin]`  |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd10    | Security / encryption / auth    | `[\ud83d\udd10 OAuth handshake]` |\\\\n\\\\n### Information & Data\\\\n\\\\n| Emoji | Meaning                         | Example              |\\\\n| ----- | ------------------------------- | -------------------- |\\\\n| \ud83d\udcca    | Analytics / metrics / dashboard | `[\ud83d\udcca Usage metrics]` |\\\\n| \ud83d\udccb    | Checklist / form / inventory    | `[\ud83d\udccb Requirements]`  |\\\\n| \ud83d\udcdd    | Document / log / record         | `[\ud83d\udcdd Audit trail]`   |\\\\n| \ud83d\udce5    | Input / receive / ingest        | `[\ud83d\udce5 Event stream]`  |\\\\n| \ud83d\udce4    | Output / send / emit            | `[\ud83d\udce4 Notification]`  |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd0d    | Search / review / inspect       | `[\ud83d\udd0d Code review]`   |\\\\n| \ud83c\udff7\ufe0f    | Label / tag / version           | `[\ud83c\udff7\ufe0f v2.1.0]`        |\\\\n\\\\n### Domain-Specific\\\\n\\\\n| Emoji | Meaning                         | Example                 |\\\\n| ----- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------- |\\\\n| \ud83d\udcb0    | Finance / cost / billing        | `[\ud83d\udcb0 Invoice]`          |\\\\n| \ud83e\uddea    | Testing / experiment / QA       | `[\ud83e\uddea A/B test]`         |\\\\n| \ud83d\udcda    | Documentation / knowledge base  | `[\ud83d\udcda API docs]`         |\\\\n| \ud83c\udfaf    | Goal / target / objective       | `[\ud83c\udfaf OKR tracking]`     |\\\\n| \ud83d\uddc2\ufe0f    | Category / organize / archive   | `[\ud83d\uddc2\ufe0f Backlog]`          |\\\\n| \ud83d\udd17    | Link / reference / dependency   | `[\ud83d\udd17 External API]`     |\\\\n| \ud83d\udee1\ufe0f    | Protection / guardrail / policy | `[\ud83d\udee1\ufe0f Rate limiter]`     |\\\\n| \ud83c\udfc1    | Start / finish / milestone      | `[\ud83c\udfc1 Sprint complete]`  |\\\\n| \u270f\ufe0f    | Edit / revise / update          | `[\u270f\ufe0f Address feedback]` |\\\\n| \ud83c\udfa8    | Design / creative / UI          | `[\ud83c\udfa8 Design review]`    |\\\\n| \ud83d\udca1    | Idea / insight / inspiration    | `[\ud83d\udca1 Feature idea]`     |\\\\n\\\\n### Emoji Rules\\\\n\\\\n1. **Place at start:** `[\ud83d\udd10 Authenticate]` not `[Authenticate \ud83d\udd10]`\\\\n2. **Max one per node** \u2014 never stack\\\\n3. **Consistency is mandatory** \u2014 same emoji = same concept across all diagrams\\\\n4. **Not every node needs one** \u2014 use on key nodes that benefit from visual distinction\\\\n5. **No decorative emoji:** \ud83c\udf89 \ud83d\udcaf \ud83d\udd25 \ud83c\udf8a \ud83d\udca5 \u2728 \u2014 they add noise, not meaning\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## GitHub-Compatible Color Classes\\\", \\\"numLines\\\": 160, \\\"startLine\\\": 1, \\\"totalLines\\\": 459}}\", \"name\": \"Read\", \"agent_name\": {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_uhzmKgvZQ52zeuC5iSqJTvOY\", \"content\": \"{\\\"type\\\": \\\"text\\\", \\\"file\\\": {\\\"filePath\\\": \\\"/home/novix/.claude_data/skills/markdown-mermaid-writing/references/diagrams/flowchart.md\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"<!-- Source: https://github.com/SuperiorByteWorks-LLC/agent-project | License: Apache-2.0 | Author: Clayton Young / Superior Byte Works, LLC (Boreal Bytes) -->\\\\n\\\\n# Flowchart\\\\n\\\\n> **Back to [Style Guide](../mermaid_style_guide.md)** \u2014 Read the style guide first for emoji, color, and accessibility rules.\\\\n\\\\n**Syntax keyword:** `flowchart`\\\\n**Best for:** Sequential processes, workflows, decision logic, troubleshooting trees\\\\n**When NOT to use:** Complex timing between actors (use [Sequence](sequence.md)), state machines (use [State](state.md))\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Exemplar Diagram\\\\n\\\\n```mermaid\\\\nflowchart TB\\\\n    accTitle: Feature Development Lifecycle\\\\n    accDescr: End-to-end feature flow from idea through design, build, test, review, and release with a revision loop on failed reviews\\\\n\\\\n    idea([\ud83d\udca1 Feature idea]) --> spec[\ud83d\udccb Write spec]\\\\n    spec --> design[\ud83c\udfa8 Design solution]\\\\n    design --> build[\ud83d\udd27 Implement]\\\\n    build --> test[\ud83e\uddea Run tests]\\\\n    test --> review{\ud83d\udd0d Review passed?}\\\\n    review -->|Yes| release[\ud83d\ude80 Release to prod]\\\\n    review -->|No| revise[\u270f\ufe0f Revise code]\\\\n    revise --> test\\\\n    release --> monitor([\ud83d\udcca Monitor metrics])\\\\n\\\\n    classDef start fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,stroke-width:2px,color:#3b0764\\\\n    classDef process fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:2px,color:#1e3a5f\\\\n    classDef decision fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#ca8a04,stroke-width:2px,color:#713f12\\\\n    classDef success fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,stroke-width:2px,color:#14532d\\\\n\\\\n    class idea,monitor start\\\\n    class spec,design,build,test,revise process\\\\n    class review decision\\\\n    class release success\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Tips\\\\n\\\\n- Use `TB` (top-to-bottom) for processes, `LR` (left-to-right) for pipelines\\\\n- Rounded rectangles `([text])` for start/end, diamonds `{text}` for decisions\\\\n- Max 10 nodes \u2014 split larger flows into \\\\\\\"Phase 1\\\\\\\" / \\\\\\\"Phase 2\\\\\\\" diagrams\\\\n- Max 3 decision points per diagram\\\\n- Edge labels should be 1\u20134 words: `-->|Yes|`, `-->|All green|`\\\\n- Use `classDef` for **semantic** coloring \u2014 decisions in amber, success in green, actions in blue\\\\n\\\\n## Subgraph Pattern\\\\n\\\\nWhen you need grouped stages:\\\\n\\\\n```mermaid\\\\nflowchart TB\\\\n    accTitle: CI/CD Pipeline Stages\\\\n    accDescr: Three-stage pipeline grouping code quality checks, testing, and deployment into distinct phases\\\\n\\\\n    trigger([\u26a1 Push to main])\\\\n\\\\n    subgraph quality [\\\\\\\"\ud83d\udd0d Code Quality\\\\\\\"]\\\\n        lint[\ud83d\udcdd Lint code] --> format[\u2699\ufe0f Check formatting]\\\\n    end\\\\n\\\\n    subgraph testing [\\\\\\\"\ud83e\uddea Testing\\\\\\\"]\\\\n        unit[\ud83e\uddea Unit tests] --> integration[\ud83d\udd17 Integration tests]\\\\n    end\\\\n\\\\n    subgraph deploy [\\\\\\\"\ud83d\ude80 Deployment\\\\\\\"]\\\\n        build[\ud83d\udce6 Build artifacts] --> ship[\u2601\ufe0f Deploy to staging]\\\\n    end\\\\n\\\\n    trigger --> quality\\\\n    quality --> testing\\\\n    testing --> deploy\\\\n    deploy --> done([\u2705 Pipeline complete])\\\\n\\\\n    classDef trigger_style fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,stroke-width:2px,color:#3b0764\\\\n    classDef success fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,stroke-width:2px,color:#14532d\\\\n\\\\n    class trigger trigger_style\\\\n    class done success\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Template\\\\n\\\\n```mermaid\\\\nflowchart TB\\\\n    accTitle: Your Title Here (3-8 words)\\\\n    accDescr: One or two sentences explaining what this diagram shows and what insight the reader gains\\\\n\\\\n    start([\ud83c\udfc1 Starting point]) --> step1[\u2699\ufe0f First action]\\\\n    step1 --> decision{\ud83d\udd0d Check condition?}\\\\n    decision -->|Yes| step2[\u2705 Positive path]\\\\n    decision -->|No| step3[\ud83d\udd27 Alternative path]\\\\n    step2 --> done([\ud83c\udfc1 Complete])\\\", \\\"numLines\\\": 100, {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_iVe7n4qLCZRnyErau7xOOi0w\", \"content\": \"{\\\"type\\\": \\\"text\\\", \\\"file\\\": {\\\"filePath\\\": \\\"/home/novix/.claude_data/skills/markdown-mermaid-writing/references/markdown_style_guide.md\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"<!-- Source: https://github.com/SuperiorByteWorks-LLC/agent-project | License: Apache-2.0 | Author: Clayton Young / Superior Byte Works, LLC (Boreal Bytes) -->\\\\n\\\\n# Markdown Style Guide\\\\n\\\\n> **For AI agents:** Read this file for all core formatting rules. When creating any markdown document, follow these conventions for consistent, professional output. When a template exists for your document type, start from it \u2014 see [Templates](#templates).\\\\n>\\\\n> **For humans:** This guide ensures every markdown document in your project is clean, scannable, well-cited, and renders beautifully on GitHub. Reference it from your `AGENTS.md` or contributing guide.\\\\n\\\\n**Target platform:** GitHub Markdown (Issues, PRs, Discussions, Wikis, `.md` files)\\\\n**Design goal:** Clear, professional documents that communicate effectively through consistent structure, meaningful formatting, proper citations, and strategic use of diagrams.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Quick Start for Agents\\\\n\\\\n1. **Identify the document type** \u2192 Check if a [template](#templates) exists\\\\n2. **Structure first** \u2192 Heading hierarchy, then content\\\\n3. **Apply formatting from this guide** \u2192 Headings, text, lists, tables, images, links\\\\n4. **Add citations** \u2192 Footnote references for all claims and sources\\\\n5. **Consider diagrams** \u2192 Would a [Mermaid diagram](mermaid_style_guide.md) communicate this better than text?\\\\n6. **Add collapsible sections** \u2192 For supplementary detail, speaker notes, or lengthy context\\\\n7. **Verify** \u2192 Run through the [quality checklist](#quality-checklist)\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## Core Principles\\\\n\\\\n| #   | Principle                         | Rule                                                                                                                                                                                       |\\\\n| --- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\\\\n| 1   | **Answer before they ask**        | Anticipate reader questions and address them inline. A great document resolves doubts as they form \u2014 the reader finishes with no lingering \\\\\\\"but what about...?\\\\\\\"                            |\\\\n| 2   | **Scannable first**               | Readers skim before they read. Use headings, bold, and lists to make the structure visible at a glance.                                                                                    |\\\\n| 3   | **Cite everything**               | Every claim, statistic, or external reference gets a footnote citation with a full URL. No orphan claims.                                                                                  |\\\\n| 4   | **Diagrams over walls of text**   | If a concept involves flow, relationships, or structure, use a [Mermaid diagram](mermaid_style_guide.md) alongside the text.                                                               |\\\\n| 5   | **Generous with information**     | Don't hide the details \u2014 surface them. Use collapsible sections for depth without clutter, but never omit information because \\\\\\\"they probably don't need it.\\\\\\\" If it's relevant, include it. |\\\\n| 6   | **Consistent structure**          | Same heading hierarchy, same formatting patterns, same emoji placement across every document.                                                                                              |\\\\n| 7   | **One idea per section**          | Each heading should cover one topic. If you're covering two ideas, split into two headings.                                                                                                |\\\\n| 8   | **Professional but approachable** | Clean formatting, no clutter, no decorative noise \u2014 but not stiff or academic. Write like a senior engineer explains to a colleague.                                                       |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n## \ud83d\uddc2\ufe0f Everything is Code\\\\n\\\\nEverything is code. PRs, issues, kanban boards \u2014 they're all markdown files in your repo, not data trapped in a platform's database.\\\\n\\\\n### Why this matters\\\\n\\\\n- **Portable** \u2014 GitHub \u2192 GitLab \u2192 Gitea \u2192 anywhere. Your project management data isn't locked into any vendor. Switch platforms and your issues, PR records, and boards come with you \u2014 they're just files.\\\\n- **AI-native** \u2014 Agents can read every issue, PR record, and kanban board with local file access. No API tokens, no rate limits, no platform-specific queries. `grep` beats `gh api` every time.\\\\n- **Auditable** \u2014 Project management changes go through the same PR review process as code changes. Every board update, every issue status change \u2014 it's all in git history with attribution and timestamps.\\\\n\\\\n### How it works\\\\n\\\\n| What                 | Where it lives                                            | What GitHub does                                                                                                                                                   |\\\\n| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\\\\n| **Pull requests**    | `docs/project/pr/pr-NNNNNNNN-short-description.md`        | GitHub PR is a thin pointer \u2014 humans go there to comment on diffs, approve, and watch CI. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"tool\", \"tool_call_id\": \"call_gmZIdy09qegolVOsNG9hF16y\", \"content\": \"\\n==============================\\n  24: # Computer Science > Computation and Language\\n  25: \\n  26: **arXiv:2508.04257** (cs)\\n  27: \\n  28: [Submitted on 6 Aug 2025]\\n  29: \\n  30: # Title:KVSink: Understanding and Enhancing the Preservation of Attention Sinks in KV Cache Quantization for LLMs\\n  31: \\n  32: Authors:[Zunhai Su](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Su,+Z), [Kehong Yuan](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Yuan,+K)\\n  33: \\n  34: View a PDF of the paper titled KVSink: Understanding and Enhancing the Preservation of Attention Sinks in KV Cache Quantization for LLMs, by Zunhai Su and 1 other authors\\n  35: \\n  36: [View PDF](/pdf/2508.04257)\\n  37: [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.04257v1)\\n  38: > Abstract:Key-Value (KV) cache quantization has become a widely adopted optimization technique for efficient large language models (LLMs) inference by reducing KV cache memory usage and mitigating memory-bound constraints. Recent studies have emphasized the importance of preserving the original precision of KVs for the first few tokens to ensure the protection of attention sinks. While this approach has proven effective in mitigating performance degradation, its underlying principles remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, it fails to address the recent discovery that attention sinks can emerge beyond the initial token positions. In this work, we elucidate the underlying mechanisms of attention sinks during inference by examining their role in the cross-layer evolution of extreme activation outliers. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between attention sinks and KV cache quantization. Based on our enhanced understanding, we introduce \\\\textit{\\\\textbf{KVSink}}, a plug-and-play method that effectively predicts sink tokens with negligible overhead, enabling more thorough preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KVSink outperforms the existing Preserve-First-N (PFN) strategy, offering more effective preservation of attention sinks during KV cache quantization. Moreover, when applied to the well-established KVQuant method, KVSink further improves perplexity (PPL) and reduces reliance on 16-bit numerical outliers.\\n  39: \\n  40: |  |  |\\n  41: | --- | --- |\\n  42: | Comments: | Published as a conference paper at COLM 2025 |\\n  43: | Subjects: | Computation and Language (cs.CL) |\\n  44: | Cite as: | [arXiv:2508.04257](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04257) [cs.CL] |\\n  45: |  | (or  [arXiv:2508.04257v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04257v1) [cs.CL] for this version) |\\n  46: |  | <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2508.04257> Focus to learn more  arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite |\\n  47: \\n==============================\\n\", \"name\": \"mcp__web_search__url2text\", \"agent_name\": \"NovixWriterAgent\"}]"}

While KV-cache quantization alleviates this cost, bit allocation between keys and values is often tuned heuristically, lacking theoretical grounding and generalizability. This paper proposes two theorems that anchor mixed-precision KV quantization in the intrinsic geometry of Transformer models. First, key projections systematically have larger spectral and Frobenius norms than value matrices, implying higher information density along the key path. Second, for any given memory budget, prioritizing precision for keys over values strictly reduces quantization error and better preserves accuracy. Empirical evaluations across various prominent LLMs and benchmarks show that key-favored allocations (e.g., 4-bit keys, 2-bit values) retain up to 98.3\\\\% accuracy compared to uniform allocations (e.g., 4-bit for both), while conserving memory. These results transform bit allocation from ad hoc tuning into a theoretically grounded, geometry-driven design principle for efficient LLM inference. Many works have studied this phenomenon in detail, proposing various ways to either leverage or alleviate it. Attention sinks have been connected to quantisation difficulties, security issues, and streaming attention. Yet, while many works have provided conditions in which they occur or not, a critical question remains shallowly answered: Why do LLMs learn such patterns and how are they being used? In this work, we argue theoretically and empirically that this mechanism provides a method for LLMs to avoid over-mixing, connecting this to existing lines of work that study mathematically how information propagates in Transformers. {"type": "trajectory", "content": "[{\"role\": \"assistant\", \"content\": \"\", \"tool_calls\": [{\"id\": \"call_YFNnX61xLh80AfG0lFUC1E64\", \"type\": \"function\", \"function\": {\"name\": \"Write\", \"arguments\": \"{\\\"file_path\\\": \\\"/home/novix/workspace/writing_space/drafts/v1_draft.tex\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"\\\\\\\\documentclass[11pt,a4paper]{article}\\\\n\\\\\\\\usepackage[margin=24mm]{geometry}\\\\n\\\\\\\\usepackage{fontspec}\\\\n\\\\\\\\setmainfont{DejaVu Serif}\\\\\\\\setsansfont{DejaVu Sans}\\\\n\\\\\\\\usepackage{graphicx,booktabs,tabularx,array,amsmath,enumitem}\\\\n\\\\\\\\usepackage[numbers,sort&compress]{natbib}\\\\n\\\\\\\\usepackage[colorlinks=true,linkcolor=black,citecolor=black,urlcolor=black]{hyperref}\\\\n\\\\\\\\usepackage{fancyhdr}\\\\n\\\\\\\\graphicspath{{../figures/}}\\\\n\\\\\\\\setlength{\\\\\\\\parindent}{0pt}\\\\\\\\setlength{\\\\\\\\parskip}{5pt}\\\\n\\\\\\\\setlength{\\\\\\\\emergencystretch}{3em}\\\\n\\\\\\\\pagestyle{fancy}\\\\\\\\fancyhf{}\\\\\\\\fancyhead[L]{\\\\\\\\small Attention sinks in small language models}\\\\\\\\fancyhead[R]{\\\\\\\\small Research idea brief}\\\\\\\\fancyfoot[C]{\\\\\\\\thepage}\\\\n\\\\\\\\newcolumntype{Y}{>{\\\\\\\\raggedright\\\\\\\\arraybackslash}X}\\\\n\\\\\\\\title{Attention Sinks in Small Language Models\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\large A Research-Backed Idea Tree and Three Testable Projects}\\\\n\\\\\\\\author{Research ideation brief}\\\\\\\\date{Evidence cutoff: 11 October 2026}\\\\n\\\\\\\\begin{document}\\\\n\\\\\\\\maketitle\\\\n\\\\\\\\begin{abstract}\\\\nAttention sinks are already documented in very small language models, making simple existence tests a weak novelty claim. This brief accompanies a persistent idea tree built through five research-and-gating rounds. Three families survived: causal function diagnostics, precision robustness, and streaming boundary behavior. The strongest finalist asks whether separate routing and value-path interventions predict held-out harm from sink removal better than attention mass alone. A second isolates transient anchor-switch shocks using position-correct factorial controls. A third tests the noninferiority of lowering sink-value precision near cache evictions, with actual byte accounting and an early termination rule for negligible savings. These are proposals, not experimental findings. The contribution of each is deliberately narrower than existing circuit analyses, sink/content metrics, asymmetric KV quantization, SubKV, KVSink, and streaming stability protocols. Novelty remains provisional; recent preprints are treated as scoped evidence, and a withdrawn quantization paper is excluded from support.\\\\n\\\\\\\\end{abstract}\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\section{Framing and research process}\\\\n\\\\\\\\subsection{What the question should become}\\\\nAn attention sink is a position that attracts disproportionate attention across later queries, often an initial token. High attention does not by itself show that the token supplies useful semantic content. Gu et al. establish the phenomenon in small models, including their tiny Pythia examples, and study its emergence under optimization, data, objectives, and architecture \\\\\\\\citep{gu2025}. StreamingLLM already includes a 160M-parameter experiment with a dedicated sink token \\\\\\\\citep{xiao2024}. Consequently, neither ``small models have sinks'' nor ``add a sink token to a small model'' is a defensible headline contribution here.\\\\n\\\\nWe use approximately 0.1--3B parameters as a working scope, not a universal definition of a small language model. The first pilots should use public 124M--1B models, followed by a current 1--3B rotary model only after a configuration audit. The important axes are architecture, training exposure, tokenizer behavior, positional encoding, KV-head sharing, and deployment backend. Parameter count alone cannot identify a mechanism. Pythia is useful because its public training checkpoints and controlled data ordering enable within-family trajectory analyses \\\\\\\\citep{pythia2023}; it does not eliminate all depth/width confounding across sizes.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\subsection{Search, filtering, and persistence}\\\\nResearch was performed through MCP paper searches, scholarly aggregation, Google discovery, paper-fulltext retrieval, and repository or publisher-page verification. Search angles covered sink emergence, small-model causal diagnostics, value versus key functions, quantization, session resets, and retrieval. Discovery is targeted and iterative, not a PRISMA-style systematic review. Broad searches returned unrelated Crossref and arXiv hits; those were excluded. The saved search cache is a discovery ledger, not an automatically trusted bibliography.\\\\n\\\\nFive expansion rounds produced three root children, two approaches per family, and three deeper finalist protocols: 13 nodes including the root, with finalists at depth three edges from the root. These are research judgments, not exhaustive priority claims.}\\\\n\\\\\\\\end{table}\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\section{Approach landscape and candidate gates}\\\\n\\\\\\\\subsection{Three families and six surviving approaches}\\\\nThe causal family contains a removal-harm predictor and a checkpoint trajectory study separating cache dependence from sink mass and outliers. No model experiments were run for this brief.}\\\\n\\\\\\\\label{fig:map}\\\\n\\\\\\\\end{figure}\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\subsection{Why these branches passed and others did not}\\\\nThe retained branches have a concrete differential question, named overlapping work, an inference-first path, and a failure criterion. The first three overlap directly with established work, the fourth has disproportionate training and kernel cost for this scoped task, and the final two risk unsupported causal or capacity claims. The incremental novelty is prospective, separate-document harm prediction across selected small-model families. Existing circuit analysis, NOP tests, compositional metrics, and attention-causal methods remain explicit baselines \\\\\\\\citep{ranmilo2026,fesser2026,papamichalis2026,franco2025}.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\textbf{Pilot.} Pin revisions of GPT-2 124M and Pythia 160M, 410M, and 1B. Use 100 development and 200 disjoint test documents at lengths 128 and 512, with three sampling seeds. Seeds vary fixture selection; they do not turn one pretrained checkpoint into three independently trained models. Keep tokenization and model-supported position conventions fixed within every paired comparison.\\\\n\\\\nAt a selected layer/head, zero only the sink value while preserving its key, perturb only the sink key using a same-layer norm-matched nonsink key, and run a sham patch. Check that the local attention weights are unchanged by the value-only intervention; later layers may change because their inputs have changed. Features include output-projected sink contribution, key-perturbation sensitivity, sink mass, and conditional content entropy. The target is excess next-token negative log likelihood (NLL) after a distinct intervention---joint removal of retained anchor states---on independent test documents. Go forward only when the paired interval for MAE improvement excludes zero and controls are consistent with the claimed attribution. Leave-family-out transfer is exploratory because the family count is small. If it fails, release the error analysis rather than claim a universal sink classifier.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\\\\\subsection{Priority 2: attribute anchor-switch boundary shocks}\\\\n\\\\\\\\textbf{Question and hypothesis.} Does changing retained anchors create a short-lived predictive loss increase beyond suffix-recomputation effects? Go forward only when an effect exceeds a development-fixed practical threshold, its interval excludes zero, and position/backend and matched nonsink-patch controls do not explain it. Otherwise reject anchor-specific attribution or identify an implementation defect.
